sections.content:
Very easy and fun course for beginners. It teach you about basic Python, including turtle as well. Turtle is covered probably as an interactive way to show how the language works, like loops, functions, if-else statement, etc. Notice it'd probably be useless for later courses though, so if you aim for practical use, you should probably apply for COMP1023 available in recent years.
Laptop is a MUST, especially for exam. They don't allow pen and paper exam format. If you plan to enrol, buy a laptop.
sections.teaching: Excellent teaching. Explain stuffs in very detail. Basically I've learnt some basic programming before so it'd be fastest to skip lectures and read notes afterwards. For beginners it'd be easiest to listen to lectures though.
sections.grading:
Good grading. I got perfect 100% grade and A+, but heard that the course is very competitive. Single mistake probably make you miss the A+.
One thing nearly ruined my midterm: my exam monitor program failed to run due to the antivirus program. One pop up appeared but disappeared quickly. I emailed Rossiter for this after exam and he requested me to his office. But at that time I did able to log in to exam monitor program due to I switched off and on the laptop. I tried different things to replicate the bug, like opening 20 chrome tabs of pdf notes, re-extracting the exam monitoring program exe file from the zip, but they didn't work. Eventually I renamed the exam monitoring program (from "exam-monitor-win.exe" to "exam-monitor-winx.exe") and successfully replicate the bug and pop-up. I immediately captured screen as proof and sent to Rossiter.
Rossiter is a very strict person, so if you encountered the same situation with me but didn't find the solution, you would eventually get a 0 mark. Be careful with that.
sections.workload:
Very light workload, if you aim for a pass or a reasonable grade. But I practice a LOT for the exams, by grinding past paper problems repetitively and time myself to build up my consistency, accuracy and speed.
How I train? Skip lectures and read notes. Once exam practice problems (midterm/final) were released, I tried to grind through them one by one. Time limit for each problem is calculated by:
((problem point) / (total point)) * time limit * 80%. This ensure you're able to do all problems using 80% of time and use remaining 20% to check your work. For those I failed to solve within time limit or got the wrong answer, I'll simply redo it the next day.
Understanding concepts is NOT ENOUGH!! Problem grinding is a MUST!! Since as mentioned, the exams are accuracy and speed oriented. They require deep complex thinking over a narrow curriculum within time pressure. Imagine, can you win grandmaster on chess by just knowing chess rules? Can you AP+ lv15 song in maimai by just knowing now notes work? This explain the importance of repetitive training.
Now about the exam problem type. There's too much of it so I won't waste time here. Basically if you watch all solution videos available, you'll eventually understand how to solve. But I need to mention some things that are not mentioned in solution videos: this course is often joked as a "typing test". When you're doing your exam on your laptop, some code are not copyable and you're expected to dry run it. Sometimes it'd be faster and more accurate and reliable if you just type the whole thing out on Python IDLE. This is allowed in exam. For longer un-copyable code you may need to shorten it yourself, only contain the critical parts and test run it.
Math is required of course. Expect DSE-levelled math. One dry run problem I can remember is to evaluate the final graph drawn by a randomly moving turtle which coordinates are constrainted by some mathematical relation, and that's equivalent to solving some inequalities to find the shape of the region representing the solution set of some simultaneous inequalities.

sections.content: This course is a very basic introductory computer science course that gives you a preliminary understanding of programming languages and the direction of subsequent required courses for computer science majors. The course uses very simple Python code as examples, leveraging the Turtle tool to briefly introduce basic concepts in programming such as variables, arrays, functions, and pointers. The overall course content is decent for freshmen, but for computer science majors, knowledge like Turtle feels quite outdated and does not provide further help in later coursework. In particular, for students who plan to take courses such as COMP2211, some array processing techniques that this course overlooks—for example, broadcasting—may be more important and commonly used in advanced studies.
sections.teaching: The instructor is quite serious about teaching, but Alex speaks very fast in class, which may be somewhat challenging for non-native English-speaking freshmen.
sections.grading: The course grading is fair. Students can decide whether the midterm exam score counts toward their final grade based on their own performance, which provides a large margin for error. The grading is not as harsh as some seniors claimed—at the time, I was told that losing any points on exams would mean no chance of getting an A, which made me quite anxious, but it actually wasn't that difficult. My scores were 100/100 on the midterm and 85/100 on the final, and my final grade was A+.
sections.workload: The overall workload of the course is relatively light. Apart from exams, there are only three or four graded lab sessions, which barely take up much of your regular study time.

sections.content: The course covers the fundamentals of Python programming, including basic syntax, Turtle graphics, loops, functions, and data types. The topics are interesting and well-suited for beginners, touching on areas like game programming and user interface design. However, the pace can be uneven; some students noted that the instructor sometimes rushes through material near the end of the term, especially before midterms and finals
sections.teaching: i think the only drawback is that attendance is not mandatory
sections.grading: The grading scheme is straightforward. Weekly lab assignments carry a significant portion of the final grade, and if you complete them carefully and understand the logic, the exams become much easier. The final exam questions are often similar to lab tasks, so practicing consistently is key. Many students worry about the exam, but in my experience, as long as you do your homework properly and review the lab solutions, you can achieve a good grade.
sections.workload: The workload is moderate—labs are manageable with TA support, but the exams are notoriously challenging.

九月份售价约为190美元，但无需购买教材即可完成学习。  
所有考核内容由学生自行负责。

统计出席人数。  
实验课仅使用课程网站提供的材料。  
每节课都有各自的实验主题。  
除作业要求的实验外，所有实验均无需提交或评分。  

课程范围：（括号内为教材章节编号）  
《编程入门与Python基础》  
+ 函数（03, 05, 07）  
+ 基本条件表达式（if..elif..else）、循环（while, for, in）（05, 06）  
+ Turtle库的基本绘图函数（02）  
+ 使用Turtle进行圆形绘画（06）  
PyGame库中的MIDI功能及时间控制  
time.sleep(0)  
+ 数据结构：列表、元组、字典（08）  
+ 列表与字符串：切片及基本操作（append(), insert(), remove(), extend(), reverse()等）（08）  
函数的结构与操作、全局变量与局部变量的区别、栈  
递归（09）  
+ 类型转换、文件读写（04, 13）  
字典的结构与操作（10）  
+ Turtle动态操作与设置：speed()、tracer()、reset()、shape()、shapesize()  
ontimer()、update()等（11, 12）  
+ Turtle的鼠标和键盘事件控制（12）  
+ 类与对象（14）  
- 作为入门课程，不涵盖全部Python函数（例如with...）
lambda,exception) 是合理的

sections.grading:
成绩权重分配：

[1] 期中考试（开卷，1小时）= 20% - 在第7周进行，考试内容涵盖课程总内容的约40%-45%。若未参加考试或包含期中考试成绩后的总分下降，则该部分权重为0%。

[2] 期末考试（开卷，2.5小时）= 40% - 在考试期间进行，覆盖全部课程内容。若学生未参加期中考试，或包含期中考试成绩后的总分下降，则该部分权重为60%。

[3] 作业1：音乐系统 = 20% - 使用Python命令行编写文本程序，读取表示乐曲的纯文本文件并输出MIDI音效。其中：
- 基础完成部分（实验3和实验4）占20%，15% + 15% = 30%；
- 额外高级功能（如列出音符和乐器信息、反转乐曲等）占70%。

[4] 作业2：游戏项目 = 20% - 使用Python Turtle界面开发SpaceInvader游戏。用户可输入敌人数量，并响应键盘和鼠标事件。其中：
- 基础完成部分（实验7和实验8）占20%，16% + 18% = 34%；  
- 额外功能（如游戏设计主题、自定义音效和精灵素材、作弊模式等）占66%。  
[*] 作业积分 = 2%（仅当作业1和作业2的总分低于40%时适用）——  
在授课过程中，讲师将邀请学生提问；若被选中并正确回答，学生可获得一个乒乓球作为奖励。课后使用该球可申请2%的作业积分。  
若作业1和作业2的总分已超过40%，则不再额外给予2%积分；  
若作业1和作业2的总分低于40%，作业总分最多只能提升至40%。
sections.workload:
一般来说，只要仔细阅读讲座、PowerPoint以及参考代码示例，就能在期中考试中获得90%以上的分数，在期末考试中获得80%以上的分数。

- 上课前应准备好PowerPoint，可以是纸质版或电脑软拷贝；如果自己没有编程基础，建议提前阅读PowerPoint的大纲。
- 下课后应复习重点内容，通常是结构（structure）、语法（syntax）等。
- 代码示例仅作参考之用，理解题目后可尝试修改代码，观察运行结果的变化。
- 实际上不需要死记硬背，要想取得高分，关键在于反复练习并尝试运行代码。
- 两份作业基本都有源代码，而且实验课的代码由讲师亲自提交，因此应对起来并不困难。
- 要记住作业必须按时提交！即使没完成也必须先提交。
- 期末考试最后几道题主要考察对数据结构（List）的掌握程度，得分的关键在于保持头脑清醒。

sections.content: This course serves as an excellent introduction to the world of computer science. It primarily uses Python to cover basic syntax, simple game programming, web design, and user interfaces. The content is both engaging and highly practical. For students with absolutely zero background in programming, this is a fantastic starting point that effectively sparks an interest in coding.
sections.teaching: Prof. Wang Shuai's teaching is highly structured and engaging. He is great at simplifying complex programming concepts and uses easy-to-understand examples to guide students through hands-on practice. The pacing of the lectures is just right, making it easy to follow along. Furthermore, both the professor and the TAs are very approachable and always willing to help answer questions after class. Overall, a great learning experience.
sections.grading: The grading scheme is clear and fair. Grades are mainly based on the midterm, final exam, and regular programming assignments. As long as you take the assignments seriously, submit them on time, and make sure you fully understand the lecture notes and practice exercises before the exams, getting a good grade is quite achievable.
sections.workload: The workload is moderate and very reasonable. sections.content:
COMP1021 is an introductory Python programming course rather than a true introduction to computer science. It's like a Coursera course. Topics include variables, conditions, loops, functions, lists, dictionaries, recursion, basic objects, and extensive use of the Turtle graphics library. Turtle, turtle, turtle and turtle.
Lectures are engaging and beginner-friendly. Gibson is really chill.
Workload is light. Only a few labs are graded, and assignments are straightforward and can be completed with reasonable effort.
Midterms were manageable but finals are much more difficult, featuring lengthy questions, tricky wording, and significant time pressure. You gonna speed up like really. Exam performance depends heavily on careful reading and avoiding careless mistakes.
I'd say this course is suitable for students with little or no programming background who want to learn Python basics. Students seeking deeper computer science concepts may find the material somewhat superficial.

The curriculum covers a wide spectrum of fundamental CS topics—ranging from game development and web programming to GUI design and computer graphics using Python.

It provides a decent overview for absolute beginners looking to get a taste of computing. However, because it tries to cover multiple practical domains in a single introductory course, it remains to be seen whether it provides enough technical depth to build solid, independent programming skills beyond basic scripting.
sections.teaching:
Given that the course target audience excludes engineering and tech majors, the instruction generally aims to keep concepts accessible, fun, and highly practical rather than overly theoretical.

The delivery seems suitable for novice programmers. That said, teaching effectiveness can vary significantly across different semesters and instructors, particularly regarding how well complex logic is simplified for non-technical backgrounds.
sections.grading:
Grading typically revolves around programming labs, short assignments, continuous assessments, and standard exams evaluating foundational concepts.

While introductory courses usually offer straightforward grading criteria, final mark distributions still depend on how strictly practical assignments are evaluated and the overall grade curve for non-CS cohorts.
sections.workload:
Since the course introduces programming concepts alongside diverse applied projects, the workload is likely moderate and steady.
For complete beginners, the learning curve for Python syntax and project assignments may require a fair amount of time initially. Conversely, anyone with prior exposure to basic coding might find the pace somewhat slow.

sections.content: A well-structured introductory programming course covering Python fundamentals, basic data structures, functions, recursion, object-oriented programming, Turtle graphics, PyGame, and simple user-interface concepts. The course does not cover every Python feature, but its scope is appropriate for beginners.
sections.teaching: The course materials are clear and regularly updated, with useful slides, code examples, and detailed lab guidance. The teaching is conducted in accessible English, although the lecture pace can be fast and the schedule may occasionally fall behind.
sections.grading: Assessment consists of a midterm, a final examination, and two programming assignments. The assignments are generally manageable because they build on lab exercises, while the examinations require a solid understanding of syntax, program structure, and data structures.
sections.workload: The overall workload is moderate. Reviewing the lecture slides, practising the example code, and completing the lab exercises should be sufficient for most students. High grades mainly require regular coding practice rather than extensive memorisation.

sections.content: The content of the course is very impractical in real life application. The course mostly just teaches python basics, but very little useful things outside of basic fundamentals you can easily learn elsewhere. I do not recommend taking this course if you are looking to actually learn and get into programming, and it might be a better option to choose COMP1023 instead. That said, this course has many topics that are rarely practical that I see as hardly useful, aside from the fundamentals you learn, such as learning how to draw using the python turtle module. The basic concepts of these topics aren't too hard to grasp, but the questions given during tests can prove to be tricky and difficult at times.
sections.teaching:
Professor LAM is very enthusiastic in teaching this course. I find his lectures to be entertaining, and rarely boring. The topics in this course are not too difficult in the first place, so it should not be too hard to grasp the basic concepts at least. However, the things you learn from the course and what appears in the exams can vary differently. For example, some easier topical questions can be easily understood from what is taught in the course, but some of the more useless topics genuinely require memorization and complex thinking that is not too well explained in the class.

Aside from that, notes are provided, and clear instructions are given in video format by the TA's, so it's not too bad.
sections.grading: I consider the grading quite fair, though it might be hard to get a good score, considering how some of the exam questions require you to think a lot given the short amount of time to complete the exam.
sections.workload: Biweekly assignments/projects. Quite standard stuff. The content of these assignments are not too hard and the TA's provide video instructions on how to complete them. Exams allow notes, and I strongly suggest to write down as much notes down of the more complex codes you write for assignments.

sections.grading: There are two types of point systems. The first type is where both the midterm and final exams contribute to the final grade. The second type only requires the final exam score to be part of the final grade. The remaining portion is from assignments. I didn't take the midterm exam because it conflicted with other exams I had. There is no make-up exam mechanism for the midterm exam in this course. So, if you really want to fully participate in the entire course, you can discuss the situation with other course instructors to see if it's possible to reschedule other exams.
sections.workload: There are a few assignments that are mandatory to participate in, while the rest are optional. The content is quite simple, and the instructions are very clear. Additionally, online guidance is provided, making the difficulty very http://low.It should be noted that even if not mandatory, the homework that needs to be submitted will also be one of the topics for the exam. Therefore, even if you don't complete the homework, you still need to review it thoroughly.

sections.content: The course provides a broad introduction to Computer Science by covering multiple areas such as game programming, web programming, user interface design, and computer graphics. The variety of topics keeps the course interesting and helps students understand how computing can be applied in different contexts. Using Python as the main programming language makes the content accessible for beginners while still allowing meaningful problem-solving.
sections.teaching: The teaching approach is generally clear and structured, making complex ideas easier to understand for students new to computer science. Concepts are usually explained alongside practical examples, which helps connect theory to practice. The pace is suitable for non-CS majors, although some topics could benefit from deeper explanations or more examples.
sections.grading: Grading is mainly based on programming assignments and assessments that reflect the material taught in class. The grading criteria are mostly clear, and the assessments are fair for students who consistently keep up with the coursework. Performance is rewarded more through effort and practice rather than prior programming experience.
sections.workload: The workload is reasonable for an introductory course. Assignments require time and effort, especially for students with little programming background, but they are manageable with consistent work. Overall, the workload aligns well with the learning objectives and expectations of the course.

sections.content: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Python programming, starting from basic syntax and control structures (if–else statements, loops, functions) and gradually moving on to data structures such as lists, tuples, and dictionaries. The use of Turtle and PyGame libraries helps students understand graphical programming, event handling, and basic UI concepts, which makes the learning process more engaging. More advanced topics, including recursion, file input/output, and basic object-oriented programming, are briefly introduced toward the end. While not all Python features are covered, the scope is appropriate for an introductory-level course.
sections.teaching: Lectures are conducted entirely in English, using relatively simple language, although the speaking pace can be fast at times. The quality of teaching materials is high, especially the lecture PowerPoint slides, which are clear, well-organized, and closely aligned with the examinable content. The course website is well maintained and updated weekly. Lab instructors explain concepts step by step and often demonstrate code directly, which is particularly helpful for students with little or no programming background.
sections.grading: Grading is based on a mid-term exam, a final exam, and two assignments. Exams are open-book but still require a solid understanding of program structure, syntax, and data structures, especially list operations. Assignments are generally graded fairly and generously if the required functionality is correctly implemented. Overall, the grading scheme is reasonable, and students who consistently follow the course materials and practice coding should be able to achieve good results.
sections.workload: The overall workload is moderate and manageable. Most learning comes from reviewing lecture slides and understanding the provided code examples rather than extensive memorization. Labs are held weekly and are mostly ungraded, but they are useful for practicing core concepts and preparing for assignments. As long as students keep up with the weekly materials and do not leave assignments until the last minute, the time commitment required for this course is reasonable.

sections.content:
If you have any coding background and are not required to take COMP 1023 and want a good grade, this course is definitely a worth-considering choice.

This course teaches Python from the basics, covering different types of variables, different types of loops and libraries (random, turtle, calendar, matplotlib).

Neither the lecture nor the tutorial takes attendance; you can decide to go or not. The tutorial is just a Zoom meeting during which the TAs will answer your questions about the lectures or the labs.
sections.teaching: Dr James Chueng's teaching is easy to understand and follow. His class is interactive, and he will have some Mentimeter questions at the end of the class, if there is time left.
sections.grading:
There are two possibilities in calculating the score; the system will take the higher one:
- Midterm (0% / 20%)
- Labs (15%)
- Assignments (20%)
- Final (65% / 45%)

Overall, I think the grading is good, because you can do the labs as long as you want.
sections.workload:
Assignments: There is a lab every 1-2 weeks, except during the first two weeks. Some labs needed to be handed in, some don't, as they are part of an assignment or just for you to have some hands-on experience on the content they taught recently. An assignment consists of two labs and additional requirements outlined on the assignment page. It may take less than an hour for each lab if you have a coding background, and 1 - 2 hours if you don't. Overall, it is not too tough because the deadline is usually 1-2 weeks after the lab is posted.

Midterm / final: Both of them are open-book and open-notes; you can bring as much as you want to the venue as long as it is not digital. So, you do not need to memorise any code. The midterm's difficulty is fine, while the final is tougher.

sections.content: General basic programming, python syntax, logic thinking, and a touch of advanced logic like recursion and object orient-ed programming, very beginner friendly

sections.teaching:
For teaching, I can only speak to Gibson Lam's teaching. I have heard stories that David Rossiter's teaching is great, but I've never attended his sessions.

Course and grading aside, I feel that Gibson Lam is actually a really great teacher. There definitely seems to be a strong passion for teaching within him and it shows well during lectures.

He himself has categorized his teaching style into "Teaching using other things instead of slides" and "Using new illustrations and examples". Which is partly true, but he does make decent use of the slides.
sections.grading:
A place where this course does redeem itself a little is the grading. The grade weightings chosen are your best of:

- Midterm 24%, Lab projects 36%, Final exam 40%
- Midterm 0%, Lab projects 42%, Final exam 58%

This does mean that, if you do poorly in the midterm, you can override it with a much better final performance.

The higher weighting of lab projects is also definitely a bonus to this course. It is completely realistic to achieve full marks in all 3 of the hand-in (marked) lab projects. This does reduce the stress of having to perform excellently in the midterms and finals.
sections.workload:
This course does not have too big of a workload. As mentioned previously, only 3 of your 6 lab projects are required to be handed in. You can definitely get away with only ever doing those 3 but do beware of the possible use of lab concepts in the final exam.

It would be difficult to severely mess up your labs if you put in any ounce of effort into them. Depending on your understanding of the course, use of AI, etc. the labs should take you anywhere from 20 minutes to 2 hours. You are also able to attend lab session to receive some guidance.

In addition, the course is also open book. You can refer to course material and personal notes during the exams. This can reduce the strain on studying for the exam and does mean the exam covers more computational thinking and logic than memorization.

So, COMP1021 may not consume much of your time, but it also won’t ignite your interest in computer science—leaving you with little more than a handful of Python scripts and a lingering sense of disappointment.

sections.content: The course introduces programming through Python in a way that is accessible to beginners. It covers basic programming concepts such as variables, conditionals, loops, and functions, along with some fun applications like simple graphics and games. The pace is reasonable for students without prior coding background, though those with experience might find some parts repetitive. Overall, the content gives a good foundation for further computer science or engineering courses.
sections.teaching: The lectures are clear and well-organised, with many practical examples shown during class. The instructor demonstrates how to apply concepts in coding exercises, which makes the material easier to follow. Sometimes the lectures move quickly, especially when introducing new syntax, but the teaching team provides sufficient support through tutorials and consultation hours.
sections.grading: The grading is fair and transparent. Assessments include programming assignments, quizzes, and a final project/exam. The assignments are manageable if you keep up with lectures, and they give good practice. Partial credit is usually awarded for effort, so even if your program does not run perfectly, you can still earn points if the logic is correct.
sections.workload: The workload is moderate compared to other engineering courses. Weekly assignments take some time, especially if you are new to coding, but they are essential for building confidence. The final project requires more effort but is also one of the most rewarding parts of the course. As long as you start early and practise consistently, the workload is very manageable.

1. Mid-term Exam (20%) – open book, 1 hr, Week 7 (~40–45% of course).
• If skipped or if counting it lowers your grade, weight becomes 0%.
2. Final Exam (40%) – open book, 2.5 hr, covers the whole course.
• If no mid-term taken, or mid-term lowers your grade, weight becomes 60%.
3. Assignment 1: Music System (20%) – command-line program generating MIDI from text files.
• Lab 3 & 4 completion = 30% of A1; extra features = 70%.
4. Assignment 2: Game Project (20%) – Turtle-based “Space Invaders” game with event handling.
• Lab 7 & 8 completion = 34% of A2; extra features = 66%.

sections.content: This is a introductory computer course about Python programming. As it is for beginner, its content is not deep and complex.  However, if you are not good at or interested in programming, you will find it's complicated or boring. For me, it arouses my interest in game programming, as there is a assignment about creating a treasure game.
sections.teaching: Every lesson has 50 mins only and it will be a new chapter, so the pitch is a little bit fast, especially to those who have not ever learn programming before. The teaching way is like a talk, explaining the ppt and sometimes demonstrates through the Python. However, it is somewhat difficult to understand. Besides lecture, there are tutorial video and zoom class. These tutorial classes are for homework guidance so they are recommended. Also, watch recordings after each lecture and do exercises released from each lecture. Practice will help for your understanding.
sections.grading: The Homework assignments account for a great percentage to the overall grading. Most of students will get full mark so the overall grading will not be bad. But remember to hand in the HW on time, as late for 1 second will be graded as 0.  Other percentage goes to Midterm and Final Exam. There are two grading scheme : count both midterm and final exam in or only count final exam . Therefore, if you perform not well in midterm, you will another chance in final. Also, the median for midterm and final is 50% to 60% only. If you meets median and get full mark in assignments, you will get at least B or B+.
sections.workload:
There are 5 programming assignments. Remember to hand in those assignments on time.  One midterm and one final exam. Also, there are two lecture classes each week, and each lesson is 50 mins only. There are also tutorial class. However, all the lecture and tutorial classes didn't take attendance and there are recordings. Therefore, the workload is super low.
But to get a better performance in midterm and final exam, do past exam paper as much as you can. The format is similar within  years. You will find those past paper from CANVAS, the instructor will release for you.

sections.content:
Fundamental Python Concepts:
Covers essentials such as if/else statements, for loops, lists, dictionaries, basic classes, methods/functions, and recursion.

Turtle Graphics:
Introduces the Turtle graphics library, which allows you to create drawings by controlling a "turtle" (think of it as a pen or brush) using code.

Difficulty:
The material should be very straightforward if you have any prior programming experience. However, take care with data types—Python is dynamically typed (and you won’t be using or tested on type hints in exams), so watch out for type-related pitfalls.
sections.teaching: The teacher has a great sense of humor, and the class is generally quite enjoyable. However, it can sometimes take extra effort to fully grasp what he's teaching.

Average: ~62.3%

Lowest Score: ~12.4%

The midterm is relatively easy, so aim to get a perfect score. However, the final exam is much more challenging; make sure you prepare thoroughly and pay close attention!

sections.content:
COMP1021 is generally an introductory course in computer programming or computer science. Here are some key aspects and comments on such a course:

### Course Content
- **Programming Fundamentals:** Introduction to programming concepts, including variables, data types, control structures (loops, conditionals), and functions.
- **Problem-Solving Techniques:** Emphasis on algorithm development and debugging skills.
- **Introduction to Programming Languages:** Often focuses on a specific language (like Python, Java, or C++) to teach core principles.
- **Basic Data Structures:** Understanding arrays, lists, and possibly introductory concepts of object-oriented programming.

### Comments
- **Hands-On Learning:** Practical coding assignments help solidify theoretical concepts and encourage experimentation.
- **Challenging Yet Rewarding:** While some students may initially struggle with programming logic, the satisfaction of solving problems can be highly motivating.
- **Supportive Resources:** Many courses offer tutoring sessions, online forums, and collaborative projects to foster a supportive learning

sections.content:
Background: DSE ICT lv5 with Elective D (programming elective) (before major syllabus change)

It is called turtle course for a reason. By the end of course, you will be so traumatized by turtle that the only thing you can remember is import turtle. I get that including turtle may seem to be more visual appealing instead of constantly staring at the boring IDLE but turtle terrorizes the questions to some stupid ass geometry problems. Some actually more relevant content (by relevant i mean in CS context) , like Object Oriented Programming and Recursion, is intended to be taught in just 1 lesson. Moreover, basic algorithms are not included in this course. These factors makes the effectiveness in introducing CS to students questionable.

TLDR: An okay introduction to python but a BAD introduction to CS

p.s. I heard there would be COMP1023 offered in 2526 fall onwards which is much better than this turtle course.
sections.teaching: Gibson is definitely a good guy. He has his own style of teaching and prepares his own materials. He is able to explain concepts clearly and maintain an engaging tone throughout the lecture, making the lectures enjoyable to attend.
sections.grading:
There are 2 grading schemes:
1. Lab work 36%, Midterm 24%, Finals 40%
2. Lab work 42%, Midterm 0%, Finals 58%

My grade:
Midterm: 51/100
3 labs: 100/100
            100/100
            100/100
Final: 74/100
Letter grade: A+

You should really be getting full marks in labs because you can literately consult everything, check answer with friends before handing in the labs.

This semester (or maybe onwards) all tests are f2f. Gibson said last semester (2425 fall) can still justify online tests due to having 1000+ ppl enrolled in the course but this semester there is only 500+ students enrolled in this course, which cannot justify an online exam. Plus the school wants to avoid having online exams if possible.

You lose the ability to use IDLE in f2f exams but you can still bring your own notes (format, content is not limited). Although the use of notes are limited to checking for syntax error and reminding yourself how to use the functions, I would still recommend you to type your own notes if you have the time since it is a good opportunity to review the lecture ppt and make sure that you know how to use the functions, codes, etc. Also, you can find the relevant information in the notes faster and easier with your own notes, which is quite important especially when time is limited

Midterm is HELL. I wouldnt blame on the f2f exams since written programming exams arent a novel thing to me with my ICT experience but you only have a little time to rush through that many questions. I bet if this midterm is done online, it would still be hell. The mean is so bad (26.53) that gibson decided to dedicate 1 lesson to explain the midterm paper (gibson expected the mean to be 50 ).

Final is much better than midterm. Maybe there is more questions (i forgor already) but i feel like more time is given per question. I can actually finish with 15-20 minutes to spare.
sections.workload: Light workload. There are 6 labs in total but only 3 of them are hand in labs. The content of the labs may be tested in midterms and finals. Plus the lab tasks arent that difficult and time consuming to complete so there is no reason not to finish all the labs.

sections.grading:
In this semester, the exams are computer-based. You can make use of Python during the exam to compute the answers. The exam is not very simple and not very hard (the time limit is tight though). But somehow, there will be a lot of people getting 100 marks. And there is always a group of people getting 0 marks. The standard deviation is quite large.

Unlike COMP2011 (where the total score is divided into many small parts), in COMP1021, each answer accounts for 6%-9% of the whole paper. You type your answers into the computer during the exam. So, the computer can catch your mistake even if you misspell one letter. (Yes, I lost 8 marks because of one letter)

For both the midterm and the final, I did not get full marks (maybe around 8X or 9X marks). I still got an A+ finally.

sections.grading:
Two grading schemes, which for this course, I don't find it much attractive.

1. Lab work 36%, Midterm 24%, Finals 40%
2. Lab work 42%, Midterm 0%, Finals 58%

The reason is purely because after this semester onwards, exams are taken in face-to-face written mode, rather than the 24 Fall Semester, exams are taken on a computer virtually. It's an open book open notes exam, but the fact that we had to use human brains to understand the few lines of code in such limited time is basically a pain to the ass.

3 lab works will be graded out of the 5-7 labs released throughout the semester. For us, it was Lab 1, 4 and 5 (Guessing game, Lava game, Music system), each worth 12% or 14% of your final score.

Midterms and finals, as mentioned, are written after so long of virtual exams. Several reasons lead to such a low mean and distribution being that right skewed, mostly being time constraints and the diverse background of students taking this course.

Score distribution (LQ/Mean/Median/UQ/High):
Lab 1: 97.5/89.3/100/100/100
Lab 4: 90/87.46/100/100/100
Lab 5: 60/72.9/90/100/100
Midterms: 13/26.53/23/34/94
Finals: 28/41.47/39/52/98

62% was my final score and got a B. Fair grading? Not my say, but at the very least, do well with your finals.
sections.workload:
The possible ways you can guarantee an acceptable score is to legit do the labs with your own hands and understanding it, as these will appear in your midterms and finals.

Second of all, start by doing past papers that are written, rather than virtual on computers. I'm not saying not to do them, but do them after you have done the written past papers. Written papers actually give you an approximate image on what the actual exam is going to look like.

Lastly, prepare your printed materials early. DO NOT THINK YOU CAN CARRY THE BOOK AND ACE THE EXAM. It is called open book, open notes for a reason. You won't expect to find your answers quickly inside the book. Prepare things like a summary on how each code works in practice, and print out the lab codes, if you feel like so.

sections.content: The course covered some basic concepts in computer science, but I felt it was a bit too focused on turtle graphics. While it was a fun way to learn, it limited the depth of other topics. We touched on important concepts like if statements, for loops, lists, dictionaries, functions, and recursion, but I think there could have been more variety. It would have been great to explore additional programming paradigms or real-world applications of Python to give us a broader understanding of the language and its capabilities. Overall, a more balanced approach would enhance the learning experience.
sections.teaching: You can definitely manage in this course without attending lectures. I didn’t go to any of them and just worked through the PowerPoint presentations and completed the mandatory labs. The materials are pretty well organized, so if you ever feel like you need clarification, you can always watch the lectures later. As long as you stay on top of the labs and engage with the content, you’ll be fine. It’s a flexible approach that allows you to learn at your own pace.
sections.grading: The grading scale in this course feels a bit off. The gap between the B and C ranges is quite wide, making it challenging to get a solid grade. Achieving an A is tough since many students already have a good grasp of the concepts before starting. The mean score for the midterm was around 50-55, and the final was similar, with a mean of about 50. On the bright side, the labs are pretty straightforward, you can usually tackle most of them in just a few hours, and some can even be finished in an hour. Overall, while the labs are manageable, the grading can be pretty competitive, especially for those aiming for top marks.
sections.workload: The course had a pretty light workload, with only 3 mandatory labs out of a total of 6. I’d definitely recommend doing the optional labs as well, since the final exam referenced some of them. If you skip those labs, you might find yourself struggling to answer some of the final questions. Overall, the labs are manageable and a great way to reinforce what you've learned, so taking the time to complete all of them will really pay off in the end.

sections.content:
Well it is an introduction course so don't expect much from it. In the course, you basically learn how to write Python with turtle, a Python drawing/GUI tool. It basically teaches you variables, if/while/for control flow, a little bit object oriented programing, and other basic things without getting TOO technical. If you already have basic programming skills, you will find this course VERY boring (personal experience).

If you are confident about your programming skills, you can just skip all the lectures and only attend the lectures before the exams just so you know how the online exams work.

===

I just noticed the course description says "students will experience a range of fun and interesting areas from the world of computing, such as game programming, web programming, user interface design and computer graphics".
... yeah that's complete bs. This course teaches, quite literally, none of that. You could argue the course does *involves* computer graphics and a bit of game programming, but you won't actually *learn* much about those things. I don't know how that gets approved.
sections.teaching: Gibson tries to be engaging, but because the course is so boring, I didn't listened to most of what he teaches. However, I think he didn't give students enough time to think about questions he asked in the class. Because of this, you might find it challenging to acquire the type logical thinking skills you need for the exam (unless you already know programming or you took ICT for the DSE).
sections.grading:
I got an A+ but I heard that the grading is pretty unforgiving if you want to get A or A+. If you make a little more than 2-3 careless mistakes (such as spelling mistakes), your A+ would be gone. However, if you are not aiming for A, the grading can actually be good, because if you messes up the midterm but nails the final, they will automatically discard your midterm result, basically giving you a second chance.

In the end I got 96 something which is an A+.

Note that, many people found the final exam this semester very difficult, and this is also evident by the mean score of *53.8*. The exam difficulty definitely varies year by year so good luck on that.

There are two different calculating grades system.
1. Mid-term Exam (open-book, 1 hr) = 20%
   -- Week 7 進行，考試範圍至約全個課程的 40% - 45%
   -- 若不赴考，或將 Mid-term 分計入後會令整體分數更低的話，佔分將變為 0%
   Final Exam (open-book, 2.5 hr) = 40%
   -- 考試週進行，考試範圍為全個課程
   -- 若之前未有赴考 Mid-term，或將 Mid-term 分計入後會令整體分數更低的話，佔分將變為 60%
  Assignment 1: Music System = 20%
   -- Python command-line 文字 program，讀取代表一段音樂的 plain-text file 以輸出 MIDI 音效
   -- 20% 中：Lab 3 & 4 基本完成部分 = 15% + 15% = 30%；額外進階功能 (列出音符及樂器資訊、倒轉音樂等) = 70%     
Assignment 2: Game Project = 20%
   -- Python Turtle 視窗介面的 Space Invader 遊戲，由 user 輸入敵方數目，並就每個 keyboard 及 mouse events 作出回應
   -- 20% 中：Lab 7 & 8 基本完成部分 = 16% + 18% = 34%；額外功能 (遊戲設計主題、自訂音效及 sprite 材質、cheat mode 等) = 66%
Assignment Point = 2% (只適用於 Assignment 1 & 2 總共得分 < 40% 的情況)
   -- Lecture 期間，lecturer 會請學生答問題；同學每次若被選中並答中，將得到一個乒乓球以作記認，下課後可憑球申請取得 2% 的 Assignment Points
   -- 若本身 Assignment 1 & 2 總分已夠 40%，將不會額外得到 2%
   -- 若本身 Assignment 1 & 2 總分不足 40%，將只會為 Assignment 總分最多增至 40%

sections.content:
The content teaches you all the basics of python programming:
- variables
- loops
- conditional statements
- functions
- basic classes and object notation
- importing basic libraries

The whole course is fully based on the turtle library and both exams allow you to bring your own pdf notes. Anyone with programming background should not struggle with any of the concepts presented throughout the course. The course however is going to be hard if this is your first try at programming and you've never taken any online courses before. The tests are not super difficult however unless you are really good at logic puzzles time will most likely be an issue to you especially if you try writing code to solve exercises during the exam.

sections.content:
Basic Python. A lot of the teaching will utilize the Turtle library since it is a drawing tool and offers visualization.

Here are some topics I can remember:

- Creating and modifying python lists, list slicing
- Moving the turtle, drawing shapes with turtle, changing the color of turtle
- Functions, utilizing functions to execute code by clicking on turtle / clicking screen / pressing certain keys
- Turtle objects
- Operators (True/False, and/or/not)
- Python dictionary
- Text and file handling
sections.teaching:
The instructors don't take attendance during lectures and allow the students to attend different lecture sections if they want to.
I was assigned to Mr. Gibson's class, and I liked his teaching style. During class he shows us a lot of exam-style questions which are similar to real midterm/final exam questions, and goes through the steps on how to solve them. Personally I found this really helpful when preparing for the exams. He also uses a lot of visuals (ex. a photo-shopped pic of himself) for class material which I found enjoyable.

I also attended some of Mr. Rossiter's classes. He spends more time on explaining the fundamental concepts to make sure the students understand the class material. He often calls out students to answer in-class questions.
sections.grading:
There are two grading systems. Your letter grade will be based on whichever system is higher:

Lab 24% + Midterm 36% + Final 40%
OR
Lab 42% + Final 58%

It is not very difficult to get full marks on lab work if you make sure there are no errors in your code and cross-check with your friends.
Both the midterm and final had a mean around 50/100 marks.

I knew how to code in Python before enrolling in this course, which gave me full marks in all labs, midterm, and final exam :)

If you know the basics of coding in Python or a different language, you will find this course quite easy. But even if you don't, it is completely possible to get an A range if you attend all lectures, make sure you understand all the PPT slides used in lectures, and go through enough past paper questions before the exams. All past papers are provided by the professors.
sections.workload:

Also the instructors offers a homework help page, which will provide most of the information you need to know to complete the homework. They are assigned once every one or two weeks. For me it took less than an hour to complete each, for my friends who were beginners they spend 2-3 hours on each.

For the exams, both are extremely hard, especially if you are not familiar with the content. A bit harsh as you score zero for a 6-7-mark question easily if you got a slight mistake. The final is insanely difficult as the mean is around 3x/100.

sections.teaching:
Tian is a new professor with Mainland background and has some Mainland accent but so far still understandable. I would say he is highly devoted to teaching as he sends Canvas messages to students in his lecture before midterm and finals to provide final tips and revision exercises (not the ones from the CSE department website but those he made himself). He also encouraged us through messages after the release of midterm results (since it was pretty scary). Pretty nice guy.

Went to sit Gibson's lecture for a few times and he is definitely brilliant and charming. His teaching is not boring at all and gives a large variety of examples to supplement the powerpoint (also examples he made himself). Nice guy, willing to answer questions.
sections.grading:
Lab gradings are based on strict marking scheme. No room for argument mostly. Not difficult to get full mark for all the labs if you follow through the instructions and tested the code before submission. No late submission allowed.

Midterms and finals are both pretty difficult this year (judged from mean score and SD). The reading-load during exam is extremely huge and the time is VERY tight. No breathing moment definitely. Both of them are divided into two sections (no significant difference in difficulty). Also, both open book, feel free to read any downloaded PDF sources or Python files from your computer, as well as the course website).
Midterm: 25 mins per section, approx. 9 questions per section.
Final: 40 mins per section, approx. 10 questions per section.
Each question may have the length of up to a page or two (for final even THREE!) and you NEED time to digest what the code is trying to do. Most questions are about filling a gap in the code so it works as intended or something like that. Not difficult if given enough time but you just don't have that luxury. All in all I find it a reading comprehension and common sense exam undercovered as Python.
Midterm CAN be omitted as there are two formulae for grading but not recommend to skip midterm since final could be even harder. Just don't bet.

Use of formula:
(Lab + Midterm + Final)
Formula 1:
36%+24%+40%
Formula 2:
42%+0%+58%
Automatically applies the higher one.

Grades (which you care about):
Lab:
Me = 100/100 (100,100,100)
Average mean = 93.67

Midterm:
Me = 82/100 (+1.09 SD)
Mean = 54.6
SD = 25.1

Final:
Me = 84/100 (+1.45 SD)
Mean = 55.5
SD = 19.6

Overall = 90.72/100 (Formula 2)
Grade = A+

A-range is highly competitive and there will always be people ahead of you unless you scored full mark for everything. I guess this year A-range was loosen (since Rossiter is leaving) but you better score more SD than me for good grades. I think from what I heard A+ cutoff is 90 this year (lucky me).
sections.workload:
Pretty light workload.
3 labs that you only need to submit your code online without the need to go to labs or lectures. Instructions of the labs are given in detail on CSE course website and should be easy to understand. If you still have questions even after reading the instructions, there will be online lab support sessions on Zoom every week for you to ask TAs.

sections.content: While turtle graphics can be an engaging way to introduce beginners to programming concepts, placing too much emphasis on it in an introductory Python course may have several disadvantages. First, it limits the scope of learning by focusing primarily on visual and geometric tasks, which may not appeal to students interested in more practical or real-world applications of programming. This narrow focus can lead to a lack of exposure to essential programming concepts such as file handling, data structures, and algorithms, which are more broadly applicable. Additionally, turtle graphics abstracts away key elements of Python syntax and logic, meaning students may struggle to transition to text-based problem-solving or larger coding projects. Overemphasis on graphics might also unintentionally foster a perception that programming is more about drawing than solving diverse problems, potentially alienating students with non-visual learning preferences or career aspirations in data science, web development, or other fields.

sections.content:
This course offers a preliminary introduction to Python programming, with a particular focus on turtle graphics. Topics covered include:  conditional statements, loops, lists, tuples, dictionaries, turtle graphics, turtle event handling, the RGB color system, text file handling, the turtle coordinate system, objects, functions, and recursion.

While the course content is well-structured for absolute beginners, offering a satisfactory introduction to basic python programming and especially turtle graphics, it might be underwhelming for those seeking a solid foundation in programming.

1. The course does not cover advanced Python features and libraries,  which are crucial for data analysis, scientific computing, and more complex programming tasks. This omission leaves students without knowledge of essential tools that do have wide applications.
2. The course lacks the rigorous training in program design, writing and testing. Although the labs are suitable examples of how to create a small program for beginners, the way they are assigned ruins the opportunity for students to practice and demonstrate programming skills.  The lab only requires creation or modification of a few lines of code in the skeleton code given, which is almost like spoon-feeding. The course simply lacks the rigor university-level courses should have.
3. The course overly emphasizes the use turtle graphics. While turtle graphics might be a fun, intuitive way to introduce beginners to programming, it is not what computer science is really about. Real programming is not just drawing stuff with turtle graphics. Interestingly, turtle as an object is introduced in the beginning of the course, yet the concept of classes and objects are introduced in the last couple of lectures. This arrangement makes the logic of the course incoherent.
4. The course name is deeply misleading. Computer science is not playing around with turtle and python. Instead, it should cover various different topics such as data structures, algorithms, computer structures, etc.
sections.teaching: Teaching quality for beginners is not bad. Cecia is nice and explains basic concepts in an engaging way.
sections.grading:
Very lenient grading in this year in terms of what percentage of students get good grades.
The course offers 2 ways of assessment and the final grade will be the higher of the two scores:
1. 36%labs+24%midterm+40%final
2. 42%labs+0%midterm+58% final
While the two ways of assessment might make it seem like the course is tolerant to mistakes, it is completely the opposite. The course is graded on a curve and many students get high scores in the exam, which means that the competition to get good grades is fierce and any unintentional mistake might kill off your A+.
The reason I still gave the grading a C despite the lenient grading this year is because I'm a little disappointed by the assessments of this course. The labs simply don't require a reasonable amount of work to get full marks. Also, the test does not really reflect coding and problem-solving skills. Instead, it is like a test on reading comprehension and familiarity with turtle. The exams are tough, but the main difficulty is not from designing and writing programs, but is from understanding many very long questions and getting them all correct within very limited time.  Be VERY CAUTIOUS in the exams and the labs. Each mistake can set you back quite a few points. The ways of assessment do not really reflect coding ability.
Here's the statistics for this year's exam:
midterm: mean:54.6, sd: 25.1
final: mean: 55.5, sd: 19.6
You are guaranteed at least an A if you get full marks in labs( be careful don't make any mistakes!) and score mean+ 1SD. Scoring a little above mean (mean +0.5 sd) in exams will get you a B+, and a little below mean is C. This is pretty good grading and the grading is indeed better than previous years, where 1 mistake in exams will approximately cost you a sub-grade, i.e. full marks=A+, 1 problem wrong=A, 2 problems wrong=A-.
sections.workload:
Extremely light workload!
Apart from exams, the only work required are the labs. 7 labs are consecutively assigned, but only 3 are required to be turned in. The code is almost given to you and it shouldn't take long. I DO recommend doing all the labs even though they're not required, because many of them appeared in the final exam this year.

sections.content:
Disclaimer: I am definitely not the intended audience for this course. I have some experience with Python in the past, am taking COMP 2711 as a freshman (which is arguably the better course to be named Introduction to Computer Science), and in the end I got full marks on all content in this course.

This course is intended for total newbies to programming in general, which is a good thing. The course title, however, is a misnomer. I would personally call it "Introduction to Turtle Graphics (and a bit of Python) (and little to none about Computer Science)".

As you can guess, this course focuses mainly on the use of the Turtle module in Python (drawing to the Turtle window, getting text and mouse input from Turtle, and a light introduction to classes by learning to use multiple turtles). It also covers a bit of Python 3.11 (loops, tuples, slicing, functions, and file handling), and barely any Computer Science topics (recursion and state diagrams).

I personally would've hoped for more about list comprehension and less about Turtle in general, since Turtle is rarely used if ever in the real world and list comprehension is 90% of what makes Python useful for all majors (yes, even business majors). The ability to just write 10 lines of code and be able to process and analyze most data you come by on a regular basis is what makes Python invaluable to learn as a beginner, and that's sadly just not covered in this course.

If you are a beginner who wants to learn Python using this course, go for it, just know that there's more to Python than turtle.forward(). If you are familiar with other programming languages and want to learn Python, this course fails to teach what makes Python stand out compared to other languages. And lastly, if you are someone super familiar with Python and programming in general, take this course for a free GPA boost lol
sections.teaching:
I've mostly went to Professor Lam's lectures, I've tried going to Professor Rossiter's lecture once. Both are great teachers for if you have absolutely no background in programming in general. Rossiter would often ask students questions randomly during lectures to make sure you are paying attention, but other than that, both professors serve no difference in their quality of teaching.

Something I've come to realize in this course is that they assume the absolute minimum in terms of your knowledge in programming, and that's a good thing. The professors would explain concepts in a really high level (high as in more abstract and less about how the computer actually processes instructions), yet also go to such detail and would provide many examples of where you might make mistakes and how to fix them.

The course website has a bunch of useful material for you to practice Python on, including a bunch of interactive examples. The lab assignments contain guided videos for literally every step of the process, and if you still have trouble with the assignments, you can go to the lab sessions where the TA guides you even more. For the more experienced, this would definitely feel like hand-holding, and it is. It can get really annoying, but it is what it is.

I will not comment any further about the lab sessions as I did not attend a single one.

sections.content:
The content is quite in-fact double edged sword. On one hand, it is extremely easy which as a result does not lead for you to spend too much time on revision, doubts clarification. However, on the other hand the content being too easy can actually decrease your motivation to study the course material properly as it is actually quite simple. For this reason, I put this course on the back burner which was quite definitely a mistake as this course's goal is not to teach you python, but to rather improve your problem-solving skills which cannot be developed with you starting to prepare a week before the exam.

The following is the content taught to us in the classes:

Introduction to Python
Introduction to Turtle Graphics
Comments and Text
Making Decisions
Loops
Lists and Tuples
Slicing
Functions
Data Types
File Handling
Dictionaries
State Diagrams
Turtle Object Creation
Event Handling
Stacks
Advanced Operators
Objects
Recursion

The turtle module was something new to me, but it really is not that tough. Once again, this course is merely interested in testing how you are able to solve the problems quickly and is not actually testing your python knowledge as quite a lot of the questions in the mid-term and final exams do not even require python.

I do think professor Lam is a good teacher as he makes the class quite interactive and he tries to lighten the class up with his jokes. He is quite open for doubts clarification by either interactions after class or through emails. However, there are people often talking while he is teaching and this is actually quite a distraction which he does nothing about. I do wish he would politely tell these students to be a bit more quiet.

With David Rossiter leaving HKUST, I think professor Lam is the best one for this course.

sections.workload:
The overall workload is actually quite little. They give a total of 7(or 8) labs, with only 3 of them being hand-in so the workload is actually quite minimal. However, I would definitely recommend students to revise each week and do the interactive examples given in each lecture and all the labs(even the non hand-in ones) as they can ask questions based on these tasks in the final.

A few tips:

* Take your labs seriously(a component where everyone can easily get 100%)
* If you get a mark cut in your lab, do check if they have marked it incorrectly by mistake as that is what happened in one of my labs and make sure that they fix it(which is what happened)
* Do NOT miss any lectures or labs as these are really helpful
* For your mid-term and final, keep all the labs open as questions can be asked from them(this was allowed for us, but rules might change each year so check with your professor)
* Take the mid-term very seriously as the final is much more challenging
* Take the past papers with a pinch of salt as they were much easier than what our final exam was, ensure that you have your concepts clear and you should be fine

sections.content:
Teaching about basic python programming & usage of turtle, including:  function, conditional control structure, loop, list & tuple, dictionary, class, recursion, file IO and usage of turtle.

These contents can help you get familiar to python programming, but actually can't help you become a 'expert' of python. You'll probably explore more about python in the future COMP classes. To be honest, you can't call this course 'introduction to computer science', but 'introduction to basic python programming'. I also don't understand why it taught about turtle. Maybe just for introducing an easy way of creating a GUI.

I have plenty experience of programming before, so these content was very easy to me.

sections.content:
B-

*Spring 2025 update: I took COMP2011, and added a section about it in grading*
Background before the course: knew pascal (outdated dse language), C#, Unity, (some) C++, (some) Python
Didn't take the C-placement test (which allows one to go directly to comp2011 programming with C++) since I want to secure GPA for CS major. Thus, I am here.

Feels more like a programming intro course suited for novices (can't really complain: I was supposed to be in COMP2011):
-Topics (python): operators, if else, while and for loops, enumerable (list, tuple, string), using modulus for sequence, function, slicing (enumerable[x:y:z]), boolean logic (limited to and, or, not), data type, text file handling, finite state, dictionary, class and object, recursion
-Topics (turtle): basic control, application of loop in graphics, handling input (click, drag, key press), using multiple turtle objects, color coding
Topics are taught in a high-level manner. By high-level, I mean more surface-level (how things behave) than in-depth (how computers cause things to behave). I guess it is for good as this approach doesn't scare off those who know less about programming prior.
While CS concepts like finite state, color coding are introduced, most topics are just programming.
I can't say that this course is entirely unrelated to CS though, since the lab projects introduce students to different fields of CS:
-Fields: digital art, game developing, digital music, and AI
-Projects: "getting started" (circle art), guessing game, sketchbook, fireworks, lava game, music system, robot thinking
The projects do look appealing, I was quite drawn in to the music one that I made some extra functions like modulating the music. On top of that, the projects aren't too tedious to complete.
However, (kinda hot take) the instructions are sometimes too hand-holding, where they gave too much hints for certain tasks (e.g. straight up the pseudocode for the part). This may hinder students from learning the mindset needed when working on the fields.
I think they should add more optional tasks for students to try out, which can put a stronger emphasis on the fields while not making the course too stressful, hence, doing a better job at introducing CS.
That being said, they provide many useful materials, including example codes, interactive examples, and most importantly previous midterms/finals with video explanation, helpful for those with less advanced background to catch up.

Extra info: only 8 (~0.57%) students got 100% total this sem

Comments:
-so many texts: so much reading to do (a question can occupy up to 3 pages), and the FOMO is no joke as misreading/misinterpreting costs (which is what happened to the 9 marks in my midterm)
-little careless tolerance: questions can weigh  6-9% in the exams with no partial credit, making the exams stressful as a careless means a noticeable chunk of marks
-TL;DR: stressful exams, even with background
-a variety of difficulty: questions can be easy as writing a line of code from giving instructions (e.g. assigning variable to a list), to hard as handling recursion for art with obfuscated variables, fairer than just being plain easy or plain hard
-better than previous exams: questions are more focused on logic than before with less blatant careless checks (= in if statement, missing quotation mark, typo), and the final doesn't have those straight up maths questions for this sem
-chiller competition than I expected (at least for a+): the pastpapers of 2022 and 2023 were quite easy, which made me think that not getting full mark might actually cost an a+. However, the final turns out to be harder this sem, with some questions being actually challenging than just having every questions easy. As mentioned, only ~0.57% of all students got full marks, implying that a+ competition is not too fierce this sem. This is why I gave B instead of C for this category. May reconsider the grading if I know more about the cutoff

Some advice:
-Grind pastpapers, they are available on the course website and some questions are straight up borrowed from them
-Complete all labs, even non-handin ones, as they can use all lab projects in questions. Make sure that you are familiar with the labs
-Careless mistakes will be your greatest enemy, while the competition is less fierce, don't let it destroy your subgrade
-Risky if you don't have time: paste the code in the question and run it using your answer if you can directly test that code, it may just be my anxiety that makes me do that

COMP2011 update:
I am aware that this course is being rebranded to COMP1023, but if you saw this, here is my recommendation whether to take the C-placement test and waiver COMP1023 or not.
*If COMP1023 is taught by Desmond Tsoi, which is likely, please do not (2024 intakes may have 1 less course, which is apparently COMP2012, with him for this, very sad)*

Otherwise, here is a few points to consider, take it with a grain of salt, as I don't know how different COMP1023 will be from COMP1021.
COMP2011 is not only about programming, but also how C++ works. It is also taught in a lower level, i.e. memory allocation, dynamic memory, etc. Just being good at programming is not enough, but you also need to actively learn C++'s inner workings if you haven't.
If your programming background is not deep enough, it is recommended that you don't waiver COMP1023.
As for grading, COMP2011's takers are very polarized: there are 2 peaks in the final's stats, one at 21-30 and one at 71-80 (out of 100). Even if "criterion-referencing" is used, it is not hard for those with a background in programming to fall in the "10-25% A-range" (ARO, 2025). Not to flex but for me, COMP2011 is an easy A+.
Since 2025 intake is department-based, it is likely that you don't need to join the best24 GPA race for CSE. If you want 3 credits for other courses (help me check if waivering COMP1023 doesn't get its credit transferred or not), or simply don't want to introduce yourself to programming again, go ahead for COMP2011. Note that its workload will be heavier  where you spend hours to days for 2 of the programming assignments.

Course content is summarized as follows, far from being an introduction to computer science:

Week 1:
Getting Started with Python
Beginning to Program Python

Week 2:
Introduction to Turtle Graphics
Making Decisions

Week 3:
Basic Turtle Graphics Summary
Loops
Examples of a Nested Loop

Week 4:
Using For Loops (with Graphics)
Sequences - List, Tuples, and Strings

Week 5:
Handling Repeated Patterns
Functions

Week 6:
More on Loops
Using Logic
More on Sequences

Week 7:
Slicing
More on Functions
Handling of Data Types

Week 8:
Midterm Review

Week 9:
Turtle Shapes
Clicking and Dragging Turtles
Clicking on the Turtle Window
Handling Key Presses
The Coordinate System
Large Turtle Graphics Summary

Week 10:
Creating Turtle Objects
Text and FIle Handling

Week 11:
Understanding Colours
More on Operators

Week 12:
State Diagrams
Dictionaries
Objects

Contrary to the course title, this course is ACTUALLY NOT an introduction to computer science. Computer science is NOT about writing programs in Python, playing with turtles (pun intended), and call it a day. Computer science IS about analyzing and designing algorithms, optimizing them, and getting to know the low-level details of your computer and how it works (instruction sets, registers, ALU, data bus, programming paradigms).

You say you teach Python, okay, I would at least expect you to teach some of the useful builtin-functions like map, filter, sum, prod (all very functional programming-like), yet, none of these were covered. At least if you cover these, I'd say the course is remotely and weakly related to computer science at all.

Multiplication of sequences by an int to repeat them probably wasn't mentioned.

Don't get me started on useful Python features. WHERE DID LIST COMPREHENSIONS GO? WHERE DID DICTIONARY COMPREHENSIONS GO?

And are you kidding me, turtle graphics? Parts of mid-terms and finals are just geometry problems disguised as Python programming problems. If you want to plot a graph, use matplotlib; if you want to play with multi-dimensional arrays, numpy's got you covered.

For context, I am also taking COMP2711 this semester (yes, and as a year 1 freshman), and it is MUCH MORE appropriate to be the PROPER introduction to computer science. More context will be in my following COMP2711 review after its final exam on 20th.

COMP1021 gives an illusion of what computer science actually is and its difficulty. This should have been a common core course instead. Yes, I'm saying computer science is difficult and it is. You'll know what is actually happening in computer science when you understand what happens further down the road of COMP, namely COMP2012, COMP3711, etc.

sections.content:
When one looks to take an introduction to computer science course, they hope to be introduced to computer science. As such, it is a huge shame that COMP1021 does not introduce you to computer science, it instead places you in the middle of the Python programming language where you have to piece everything together yourself.

Exploring the content, the following topics are covered:
- Installing python, the python shell, print(), input(), variables, type casting, the random module, python files.
- Turtle graphics, moving, colours, etc.
- Selection/decision statements (if, elif, else), comparison operators, indentation
- Looping (for, while)
- Python sequence types (List, tuple, string)
- The modulus operator (%)
- Functions
- Slicing, 2D/3D structures (with lists)
- Data types
- Turtle shapes, click and drag events, key events, the turtle coordinate system
- The RGB colour system
- State diagrams
- Dictionaries
- Objects
- Recursion

This is a pretty compressive list of topics if you aim to become acquainted with Python. But therein lies the major problem: these topics, while useful for basic scripting, are woefully insufficient for understanding the fundamentals of computer science.

Nothing about how computers work, nothing about computer history and paradigms, nothing on anything to do with foundational computer science. Such as disastrous and ill-fully narrow course this is. Computer Science classes at high school teach this stuff yet the university level course couldn't think to include it.   

First time students are left with a mountain of content and no idea how it works at any level below the surface. Students complete this course only knowing how to construct bare Python scripts.

It is also very important to bring up the unnecessarily extensive use of Turtle graphics. It is clear the designers of this course imagined that the fun interactivity of Turtle graphics might make students interested in the course. However, what starts off as a playful learning tool turns into an overused gimmick. Students are guided into using this heavy object-based module from the start, only covering objects in small detail right at the end of the course. Turtle Graphics becomes less of a tool for learning and more of a colorful distraction, a facade masking the course's lack of depth.

If the content of this course is bad, the examinations are certainly terrible. Never have I seen such devilish and unreasonable examination questions in my life. One question from a midterm read as follows:

"A quadrillion is one followed by 15 zeroes. What is a quadrillion divided by 2? Use Python to work it out."

Only a true genius could conjure up such a work of art. How could this actually be testing anything useful? This just tests a student's ability to type out 15 zeroes under the stress and pressure of the examinations. Ridiculous.

While some exam questions are intuitive and interesting, the majority stand to bring you a deep sadness. You are constantly second guessing yourself as the questions are riddled with gotchas. It is as if those who wrote the exam sat laughing, smugly taunting students as they put these questions together.

In the end, this course is a true disappointment at an opportunity to ignite curiosity and wonder in the computer science field. Many assume a science and technology university to have a truly captivating computer science course, but this just isn't the case. It feels that many students take this course, finish it, and have no further interest to pursue computer science.

COMP1021 demands your respect, claiming to introduce computer science but instead delivers an accelerated Python bootcamp, over-reliant on Turtle Graphics to mask its lack of substance. It's playing us for fools.
sections.teaching:
I can only speak to Gibson Lam's teaching. I have heard stories that David Rossiter's teaching is great, but I've never attended his sessions.

Course and grading aside, Gibson Lam is actually a pretty good teacher. There definitely seems to be a strong passion for teaching within him and it shows well during lectures.

He himself categorizes his teaching style as a style which "Teaches using other things instead of slides" and "Uses new illustrations and examples". But we must be real and ground ourselves in reality, he most definitely makes extensive use of slides.

A first-time learner of computer science may struggle understanding Gibson Lam as he goes into an internal monologue during his teaching, covering important novel concepts incredibly quickly and without much afterthought. That being said, if you can understand his fast spoken English and swift topic switches, learning from Gibson Lam can be both rewarding and interesting.
sections.grading:
An area this course redeems itself a little is the grading. The grade weightings chosen are your best of:

- Midterm 24%, Lab projects 36%, Final exam 40%
- Midterm 0%, Lab projects 42%, Final exam 58%

This does mean that, if you do poorly in the midterm, you can override it with a much better final performance.

The higher weighting of lab projects is also definitely a bonus to this course. It is completely realistic to achieve full marks in all 3 of the hand-in lab projects. This does reduce the stress of having to perform excellently in the midterms and finals.

However, all of this doesn't quite matter if this course is graded on a curve, for which it is. Despite being an introductory course, you are against the full range of students. There will be students who have never studied computer science and students who have been programming since they were 5. This makes it difficult to achieve top grades in the course and feels to be demotivating for new students who actually were interested in computer science.
sections.workload:
The workload in this course is perfectly reasonable. Only 3 of your 6 lab projects are required to be handed in. You can definitely get away with only ever doing those 3 but do beware of the possible reference of the non-hand-in labs in the exams.

It would be difficult to severely mess up your labs if you put in any ounce of effort into them. Depending on your understanding of the course, use of AI, etc. the labs should take you anywhere from 20 minutes to 2 hours. You are also able to attend lab session to receive some guidance.

In addition, the course is also open book. You can refer to course material and personal notes during the exams. This can reduce the strain on studying for the exam and does mean the exam covers more computational thinking and logic than memorization.

In all, COMP1021 may not consume much of your time, but it also won’t ignite your interest in computer science. Thankfully though, it does seem to only be uphill from here.

sections.content:
The Python library turtle was an engaging and surprisingly effective tool for the course. At first glance, it seemed like a basic graphics tool for beginners, but it proved to be much more than that. By using turtle, we were able to visually understand programming concepts such as loops, functions, and even event-driven programming, which made the learning process both interactive and enjoyable.

One of the standout aspects of learning with turtle was its ability to train a programmer's mindset. It encouraged logical thinking, problem-solving, and debugging, as we had to figure out how to make the turtle move in specific patterns. The process of troubleshooting errors and refining code to create precise results felt similar to real-world programming challenges, which added depth to the learning experience.

Overall, the course successfully used turtle to not only teach Python basics but also to develop a strong foundation in programming logic and creativity. I would recommend this course to anyone starting their journey in programming or looking for a fun way to strengthen their skills.
sections.teaching:
The Python library turtle was a fascinating part of this course, and although I didn’t attend the lectures, I was able to learn effectively by studying the PowerPoint slides on my own during my free time. The materials were well-structured and clear, making it easy to follow along independently.

Using turtle to create shapes and patterns provided a hands-on way to understand programming concepts like loops, functions, and logic. It also allowed me to practice debugging and problem-solving, which are critical skills for any programmer. Even without attending classes, the combination of detailed slides and practical coding exercises made the learning process both engaging and manageable.

I appreciate how the course used turtle not just as a graphics tool but as a way to cultivate a programmer’s mindset. It’s a great resource for anyone looking to learn Python in a visual and interactive manner, whether through lectures or self-study.
