如果你志在CS又没有基础，不要指望这门课能帮你入门CS。
这个课真的非常垃圾！首先上大学开始第一学期只学python就很让人费解，而这门课的内容更是离谱。讲完循环控制，就直接跳到海龟作图，然后下半学期直接讲游戏设计，还是用功能受限制的海龟模块来完成。这门课就像是把好几种教程的第一节课拼在了一起，看似覆盖了好多模块，但全都只涉及最基本的内容、语法。比如讲GUI（图形用户界面），竟然是用海龟作图完成的，而且一节课就完了，我学完后无法建立对这种功能的理解，只是看懂并且能够重复老师所展示的代码，此外毫无用处。
对于大部分课，我的感受是老师在为了完成一个项目而教我实现目标所需的每一步，所以我的知识掌握是一条飘忽不定的细线，这里学一点，那里学一点，最后照葫芦画瓢写出讲过的程序但对于python的入门、库的调用实在没有帮助。python是最热门的编程语言，可以在精简的程序里实现强大的功能，但想要实现那些功能就避不开进阶内容的学习，而这门课只是为了让我们感受到编程的趣味而教我们写华而不实的皮毛技巧罢了。
如果你有进入CS的目标，想要刷绩点，请慎重选择，拿高分不难但是很看运气和考试状态，因为大部分人和你一样能拿高分。
如果你只是想凑够ccc的学分，或者想接触一点编程，那学这个课很好，你会感兴趣的。

The most terrible course I have taken. This course focuses on python, in order to lead us into the world of programming. But I believe this goal is hardly achieved. The content involves basic input and output, if/while/for control, function, turtle graphic, GUI, text input and output and so on. It seems like rich content, but you will not be able to learn the key concept of those functions, just be able to repeat what teachers did in class and create slightly difference. If you don't want to study computer science of related major at all, then you can choose it to fulfill your ccc requirement. If else and you have a thirst for knowledge, I recommend you to take COMP2011 since you just need to do some preparation and pass the test.

sections.grading:
由于从课堂中我们没办法学习到更实际的内容，在思维上也没有难度，老师们大概也知道这点，因此考试的实际难度很低，基本上看过ppt就都会做。但是为了拉开分数给龟，考试事件非常短，题目阅读量比较大而且在各种额外的限制条件上设坑，这需要在考试中快速阅读并得出答案。不太容易得满分，并且你如果具有编程基础也没有什么优势。

The exams are terrible too. Since you are not taught with real knowledge, the exam is easy and doesn't require you to think deeply. But the time is really tight so that you need to be concentrated during the exam and it's not easy to get full score.

There are two types of grading system (the one with highest marks will be chosen for the student):

Lab projects 36%

Absolute grading, it is easy to achieve high grades.
Expect the cutoff to be high because this course is easy.

There are 2 methods to count your total score; whichever is higher will be automatically applied.
Method 1: 24% Midterm + 36% Lab + 40% Final
Method 2: 42% Lab + 58% Final

My score:

Midterm: 100/100
Average (excluding zeros): 89.6
Average (including zeros): 82.6
Standard deviation (excluding zeros): 15.6
Standard deviation (including zeros): 28.3

Lab: 292/300
Some of the labs (in this semester, 3 out of 7 labs) will count toward your grade. Everyone should get full marks unless you made careless mistakes like me and did not check the program you submitted.

Final Exam: 81/100
Average (excluding zeros): 55.5
Average (including zeros): 53.8
Standard deviation (excluding zeros): 19.6
Standard deviation (including zeros): 21.5

Total score using method 1: 91.44
Total score using method 2: 87.86
Grade: A+
As I don't have any programming bacckground, this is a really good grade.
Somehow in this semester the cutoff isn't that high, btw I lost 13 marks (2 questions) in the final exam due to mistyping 1 letter and not adding commas between each answer.
sections.workload:
I would consider the workload to be pretty low. Each week you will have 2 50-minute lessons, and sometimes you need to do some labs. There is 1 midterm and 1 final exam.

For labs, there will be clear instructions on what you need to do, and there will be videos teaching you how to do it. Each lab will take you about an hour, and you can do it at your own time.

In the timetable, there will be a section for lab, but you don't need to attend that section as it is for you to ask questions to TA on Zoom, although I never attend that section.

The midterm, final exam, and some of the labs (in this semester, 3 out of 7 labs) will count toward your grade. I believe doing some past papers, attending each class, and finishing all labs are enough for your revision.

sections.content: This course covers the basics of Python programming, including fundamental concepts such as if/else statements, for loops, lists, dictionaries, basic classes, methods/functions, and recursion. Additionally, the course introduces Turtle graphics, a Python library for drawing pictures using "turtles" (essentially code-driven pens). The content is straightforward for those with some programming background but still valuable for reinforcing core concepts.
sections.teaching: for students who already have programming experience, the lectures might feel redundant and slow-paced. If you are confident in your skills, you might find it more efficient to learn independently and skip some of the classes.
sections.grading:
The labs are generally straightforward but require careful attention to detail.

The midterm exam is considered relatively easy if you are careful and take time to check your answers.

The average score for the midterm is around 71.9, with a standard deviation of 21.4. However, the final exam is quite challenging, at least for me. It has limited time for double-checking answers and includes tricky questions designed to trip up students. The average score for the final is only 48.57, with a standard deviation of 19.29.
sections.workload: The workload for the course is quite manageable. With only seven labs and one introductory lab, and three of these being graded, the overall time commitment is relatively light. Non-graded labs are optional, but it is advisable to review them as they may contain material that appears in the final exam.

sections.content: The Python course covers a comprehensive range of topics essential for developing proficiency in the language. It starts with an introduction to Python syntax, data types, and control structures. Students then delve into more advanced concepts such as functions, modules, file handling, and object-oriented programming.
sections.teaching: The course is taught by an experienced instructor who effectively combines lectures, demonstrations, and hands-on exercises to facilitate learning. The lectures are engaging and the instructor encourages active participation from the students, fostering a dynamic learning environment. The instructor is also readily available during office hours and provides prompt feedback on assignments, ensuring that students have the necessary support to grasp the material.
sections.grading: The course assessment consists of a midterm and a final exam, as well as a series of biweekly lab assignments. The exams test the students' understanding of the core Python concepts and their ability to apply them in problem-solving scenarios. The lab assignments provide an opportunity for students to practice their programming skills and consolidate their learning. The grading criteria are clearly communicated, and the instructor provides detailed feedback on the assessments, allowing students to identify their strengths and areas for improvement.
sections.workload: The course demands a significant time commitment from students, with a combination of lectures, labs, and independent study. The biweekly lab assignments require a substantial amount of time and effort to complete, as they involve writing and debugging code. Additionally, the midterm and final exams require thorough preparation and revision. While the workload may be challenging, it is well-aligned with the course objectives and provides students with the necessary practice to develop proficiency in Python programming

The first way :
Midterm 24%, Lab projects 36%, Final exam 40%

Midterm 0%, Lab projects 42%, Final exam 58%

Before I enroll in this course, I have heard a lot of people saying that the mean is really high so even if you answer only one question incorrectly in the exam, you will fail to get an A+.  But the reality really surprise me.

First of all, the mid term exam in this semester is easier than the past paper(quite a lot). After the exam, I believe that there will be a lot of students getting something like 90 to 100 marks. However, the mean of the mid-term exam is 52 only. So the mean is definitely not as high as people's thoughts.

The most interesting part is the final exam. Do you know what is the mean of the final exam?  It is 33! (fyi the full mark is 100). However, the difficulty is similar to the past paper that are given to us. Therefore, even I get a score that is lower than 50 in the final exam, I still get an A (I don't do well in the mid-term and labs). Therefore, I think people overstating the difficulty to get a good grade.

sections.content: This course offers a gentle introduction to Python programming, covering essential concepts like conditional statements (if-else), loops (for and while), and basic turtle graphics commands. It’s designed to be accessible yet engaging, ensuring that beginners can grasp the fundamentals without feeling overwhelmed by complexity. Through interactive lessons and practical exercises, students will learn to write simple programs, enabling them to understand the core principles of coding and computational thinking. The turtle module, in particular, will allow them to visualize their code in action, making the learning process both fun and informative.
sections.teaching: The program is well-suited for beginners, offering a solid foundation in the basics of the subject. It is highly recommended that newcomers enroll in the lessons, where experienced instructors will guide them through the learning process at a comfortable and gradual pace, ensuring a thorough understanding of the material.
sections.grading: The primary issue with the course is its elementary level, which allows individuals who already possess foundational knowledge to achieve high scores with relative ease. Consequently, the grading curve is set so steeply that even securing a 90% mark may not suffice to guarantee a top grade or distinction, as the majority of the class is performing at a similar level.
sections.workload: While the course demands are not excessively stringent, it is crucial to consistently monitor your progress and ensure that all laboratory assignments are submitted punctually. Staying on top of these requirements will help you maintain good standing in the class and avoid any last-minute rushes that could impact the quality of your work.

sections.content:
Format:

Lectures: 2 sessions per week, around 1 hour each; attendance not counted.
Lectures only use PowerPoint slides from the course website, which are updated weekly.
A textbook written by the lecturer (《Interactive Python Programming for Beginners》, September 2016, around $190) is recommended but not required to complete the assessments.
Labs: 1 session per week, around 2 hours each, attendance not counted.
Labs only use materials from the course website, with a lab task for each session.
Except for the labs required for assignments, no other labs need to be submitted or graded.
Course Coverage: (textbook chapter numbers in brackets)

Programming fundamentals and basic Python functions (03,05,07)
Basic conditional statements (if...elif...else), loops (while, for...in) (05,06)
Basic drawing functions in the Turtle library (02)
Drawing with Turtle using loops (06)
PyGame library's MIDI functionality and time control (time.sleep())
Data Structures: List, Tuple, Dictionary (08)
List and String: Slicing and basic functions (append(), insert(), remove(), extend(), reverse(), ...) (08)
Function structure and operations, global vs local variables, stack, recursion (09)
type(), file read/write (04,13)
Dictionary structure and operations (10)
Dynamic Turtle operations and settings: speed(), tracer(), reset(), shape(), shapesize(), ontimer(), update(), ... (11,12)
Turtle mouse and keyboard event control (12)
Class and Objects (14)
As an introductory course, it is reasonable not to cover all Python features comprehensively (e.g. with..., lambda, exception)
sections.teaching:
Pros:

All-English instruction, though vocabulary is concise and pace is relatively fast
Independent course website (http://course.cse.ust.hk/comp1021)
Course materials including PowerPoint PDFs (color and grayscale versions), code examples are published a week in advance on the website
Lab instructors explain each step and its significance in detail based on website materials, providing actual code when needed, so students who don't understand the code can copy it during labs
Cons:

The first few lectures did not complete the content for that session, causing the teaching progress to lag behind
Lecturers are accustomed to using English, and their pronunciation is sometimes inaccurate

sections.content: the course offers a solid foundation in computer science. The content is well-structured and comprehensive, providing a good overview of the subject matter. However, the course heavily relies on the turtle library module for its programming assignments. While turtle is a great tool for beginners to grasp the basics of programming, its practicality in real-world applications is limited. In my opinion, the overuse of turtle does not adequately prepare students for future challenges in the field of computer science.
sections.teaching: teaching style is commendable and he consistently goes above and beyond to ensure students understand the material. He provides additional exercises in every meeting, which greatly aids in reinforcing the concepts taught in class. His dedication to teaching and his ability to make complex topics understandable are truly appreciated.
sections.grading:
The grading system in COMP 1021 could use some improvements. The course follows a curve, which can be challenging and may not accurately reflect a student’s understanding of the material.

There are two grading schemes: one where the final exam constitutes 58% of the grade and lab work makes up the remaining 42%, and another that includes the midterm. This can create confusion and inconsistency in how students’ performance is evaluated.
sections.workload:
The workload for COMP 1021 is manageable. The course includes five labs that are quite straightforward, making it easy for students to grasp the concepts. The labs are well-structured and provide a good balance between challenge and achievability.

Moreover, the lab assistant is very helpful and approachable. They provide valuable guidance and are always ready to assist students in understanding the lab exercises. This support greatly enhances the learning experience and makes the labs an enjoyable part of the course.

sections.content:
Syllabus of the course:
- Fundamental functions of Python (variables, Booleans, loops, lists, tuples, strings, slicing, functions, dictionaries, text and file handling in Python, objects)
- Turtle graphic (basic drawing codes, creating new "turtle", dragging and clicking processes, key presses processes, coordinate system, colour changing)
- Basic logic (state diagram, recursion)
The content is quite interesting even if you are a beginner of computer programming like me. Most of the content is easy to understand. Of course, if you have learnt Python before, this course will be very easy for you.
sections.teaching:
Gibson is a great instructor. He has a funny accent and often makes jokes during lectures.
His teaching pace is quite fast. You need to fully pay attention to understand and catch up with what he is saying. Normally, he seldom uses PowerPoint for lecturing. Instead, he will create some examples and demonstrate the functioning of the codes, You can still understand the concepts effectively by following his logical flow.
The TAs will hold online assistant sessions (which are actually the lab sessions as shown on the timetable) for every lab. They give a lot of help to students. So it is quite easy for you to complete the labs and understand the concepts.
sections.grading:
The assessment plan of the course:
Formula 1: Labs (36%) + Mid-Term (24%) + Final (40%)
Formula 2: Labs (42%) + Final (58%) (Mid-Term not included)
Statistics:
Lab 1 Mean: 94.4/100
Lab 5 Mean: 90.9/100
Lab 6 Mean: 92.4/100
Mid-Term Mean: 47.2/100
Final Mean: ~66/100
My score: Full mark in all the 3 labs, 41/100 in Mid-Term, 82/100 in Final, 89.5/100 in total (using formula 2)
They will use the highest score from one of the formulas as your final score. It means that you don't have to worry if you get a bad grade in the Mid-term.
I don't think that this course really gives out good grades. I could only get a B+ with this total score. I got some statistics from others that 91 could only get an A- and you had to have 98 to get an A+. Perhaps there are too many smart students in this course.
Don't make careless mistakes in the exams anyway. They can really cost a lot in this course.
sections.workload:
Theoretically, there are 7 labs to do, but only 3 of them are hand-in labs. So there are very little things to do.
They will provide interactive examples for you to understand the functions of different codes. Before exams, past papers will also be uploaded to the system so that you can be familiar with the exams. I strongly suggest completing them, especially if you are revising for exams. You don't have to do many things in this course anyway.

sections.content:
While the course content itself was informative and comprehensive, I must admit that the exam posed a significant challenge. In this review, I will delve into the positives and negatives of the course, providing an unbiased perspective for prospective students.

Positives:

Comprehensive Content: The course covered a wide range of topics related to Python, ensuring that participants gained a solid foundation in the subject matter. The content was well-structured, logically presented, and provided valuable insights into various aspects of python.

Knowledgeable Instructors: The instructors were highly knowledgeable and experienced in their respective fields. They demonstrated a genuine passion for teaching and were always willing to answer questions and clarify doubts. Their expertise contributed to a better understanding of complex concepts and facilitated meaningful discussions.

Practical Approach: The course emphasized practical application, enabling students to develop real-world skills. Hands-on exercises and projects were an integral part of the curriculum, allowing participants to gain valuable experience and enhance their problem-solving abilities.

Negatives:

Difficulty of the Exam: Undoubtedly, the most challenging aspect of the course was the exam. The exam questions were extremely difficult, often requiring an in-depth understanding of complex concepts and their practical application. While a certain level of difficulty can be beneficial to test one's knowledge, the exam's difficulty level seemed disproportionately high compared to the course content.

Lack of Exam Preparation: Although the course material adequately covered the subject matter, there was a noticeable absence of specific exam preparation. Some students may have benefited from additional guidance and resources to better prepare for the challenging exam.
The content of the course is pretty introductory, basic python stuff. Although there is an emphasis on using turtle graphics which in my opinion is not very useful.

The exam does not at all test your coding knowledge or ability rather it tests your arithmetic skills and how quickly you can solve problems. A simple silly mistake under huge pressure and you've lost your grade. I don't think the course is well designed in this area, as it does not at all reflect your programming skills. The time given for the exam is extremely short.

Though the good thing about the course is that there are two grading methods, so even if you mess up your midterm, you can still be saved in the finals.
sections.workload: The workload for this course is very little. You just need to submit 3 assignments and even those can be done in just a couple of hours if you know the content well.

After the mid-term of the course, usage of functions, logic, key press, drag, .txt saving mechanism, objects and recursion will be mentioned.
However, if you have explore more about it on the Internet, you will found out that the whole course is just a very very small part of Python, of which is very far away from making graphics or even some basic applications.
sections.teaching:
Well, the teaching style of every teacher is very different. Some of my friends might think that Professor Rossiter might be wasting too much time in explaining the examples (which is not given to the students for further exploration), while always expecting every students knows what is the missing part of the examples (if you answer them incorrectly, you might feel his disappointment through his response)
For Professor Lam, his teaching would be more focused on explaining the working principles of the commands that he is using, and the codes are very simple to understand, which is very helpful for beginners of using Python

Actually, I did not really listen much about the teachings after the first half of the course, since most of the thing can be learnt by yourself by watching the PowerPoints

VERY IMPORTANT TIPS
Pretty much the resources for practicing is very limited, so if you wish to completely know what you are doing with the codes, try this free platform for practicing with some more practical situations:
https://www.codewars.com
sections.grading:
I think this is the main factor for choosing this course, especially for the 1st year student of SENG (since GPA can be a high priority for choosing course in the first year)
There are two types of grading system (the one with highest marks will be chosen for the student):

Midterm 24%
Lab projects 36%
Final exam 40%
OR
Midterm 0%
Lab projects 42%
Final exam 58%

you may already see that you can have a very different approach for getting good grades in this course. Unfortunately, in my semester, basically the mid-term would force you to use the second grading method, creating a extremely high pressure in the finals.

Well, for me,
I got full marks in the labs
Then I got like 60% in the mid-term (a very high paced exam, with lots of information to analysis in a very short time, cheat sheet doesn't help too much cuz you don't even have the time to take a peek on them)
For the finals, I got full marks on it, since the difficulty is lowered and I found out there are better methods to practice coding
so by the second method, I got 100% for the overall score of the course and get a A+

tbh I do not support this kind of grading system, cause many people just go all in on the finals and just loses, while some of the people just walk away with a very good grade using the first grading system. Pretty much you will feel like gambling with your grades without even knowing it.
sections.workload:
There are 3 assignments (labs) that needs to be done. Basically like making a number guessing game, a music system that uses .mp3 files as notes, a robot for completing a maze using right hand rule.
Don't have to really worry much about them, cause most of the hard part is given by the teachers and there is plenty of time for you to ask the teacher assistants to debug your codes.
Personally, each assignment costs about 3 hour to finish, including watching the videos given, and the duration of the assignment is around 1 - 2 week, so if you manage your time well, you will be able to finish them perfectly

sections.content: The course content is well-structured and easy to follow, as it covers the fundamental concepts and skills of programming and computing. The course also adapts to the situation and adjusts the syllabus accordingly, such as skipping the object-oriented part due to the shortened semester.
sections.teaching: The course instructor, David, is humorous and kind, and he makes the lectures lively and interactive. He also provides clear explanations and examples for the topics. The teaching assistant, Jimmy, is very helpful and responsive, and he gives useful guidance and feedback for the assignments and projects. The online forum is also a good place for students to ask questions and share ideas.
sections.grading: The course grading is fair and reasonable, as it reflects the students’ performance and effort. The course assessment consists of quizzes, assignments, projects, and a final exam. The quizzes are short and frequent, testing the students’ understanding of the lecture materials. The assignments are fun and challenging, requiring the students to apply their knowledge and skills to solve problems. The projects are creative and rewarding, allowing the students to design and implement their own games, websites, and graphics. The final exam is very difficult and stressful, with long questions and time constraints.
sections.workload: The course workload is light and manageable, as it is consistent with the credit hours and the level of difficulty. The course requires students to spend about 8 hours per week on average, including attending lectures, tutorials, and labs, completing quizzes, assignments, and projects, and studying for the exam. The course is not too demanding or stressful, as long as the students plan ahead and work steadily.

sections.teaching:

If you DO want to attend lectures however, this course lets you attend whatever sections you like (no matter the instructor or timeslot), since no attendance is taken. ATTEND DAVID ROSSITER'S LESSONS. He actually tries to engage his students and makes his lessons interesting.
sections.grading:

The time is very TIGHT actually since each question contains a lot of text. So make sure that you don't take more than 3~5 minutes to answer each question.

sections.content:
Basic Python and Application of Turtle Graphics Library:
- Drawing basic shapes with turtle
- Variables (local & global)
- Flow Control: If statements, while and for loops
- Lists
- Lists slicing
- Tuples
- Strings
- Dictionaries
- Arithmetic Operations (+, -, *, /, %)
- Data Types conversion
- Functions
- Events Handling (react when the user drag, click or enter something)
- RGB colors in turtle
- File Handling (opening, reading and writing files)
- Text handling (splitting text, trimming white spaces etc)
- Objects & Objects Oriented Programming (just basic info, no complicated stuff like inheritance)
- State Diagram
- Recursion

Labs:
There are 7 labs in total this semester, need to hand in 3 of them. Others are optional, but the content may appear in the exams.

You can work on the labs at your own pace before the deadline. Although there are assigned time slots for labs, they are just for lab support sessions on Zoom. No need to go if you do not have questions.

Exams:
- Midterm
- Final

There are lots of revision materials for this course. Tones of interactive examples and past papers provided before the exam. Most of the past papers come with a video explanation, which is quite useful if you get stuck in a question
sections.teaching: Prof. Gibson is an enthusiastic and interesting professor, I seldom feel bored when attending his lectures. He also go through one or two exam type question(s) in each lectures, quite useful if you would like to get familiar with the question types that will appear in exams (not sure if other sections also include this)
sections.grading:
Perhaps absolute grading with adjustments based on the overall result.

There are two grading methods:
- Labs + Midterm + Final; or
- Labs + Final
So midterm is kinda optional if you are very confident that you will do well in the final.

My results:
Labs: 100
Midterm: 67 (I screw this up by wasting too much time on a question that is wrong)
Final: 100
Grade: A+

sections.grading:
# Course grading policy #
There are two ways of grading, and they will choose the one that gives you the higher score. This means that if you didn’t do well in the midterm, you can all in final. For this semester, it seems that the midterm is almost useless because it was much harder than final and most people use the second grading scheme.
Scheme 1: midterm 24% + labs 36% + final 40%
Scheme 2: midterm 00% + labs 42% + final 58%

# Some statistics #
Almost everyone can get full in labs, including me.
Midterm : mean = 47.2/100 || sd = 21.2 || mine = 100
Final : mean = roughly 66/100 || mine = 94
Overall : mine = 97.6% -> A
I’m definitely not satisfied with this letter grade because I only got ONE question wrong in the final exam. In this semester, it seems that only those who get full in overall can get A+. Bad grading.

Labs are easy because there are clear instructions and grading schemes. You can follow the instructions step by step and easily receive full marks.
Midterm is much harder than final this time. As a result, for those who don’t have programming background, all in final is not a bad choice in this semester. However, I think the exam actually does not test your programming ability. The important thing is to avoid careless mistakes. I think they could have designed the exam problems more properly. What’s more, online exams brought many problems. Be careful, otherwise you may get a penalty.

说好龟是因为零基础也能轻松进A range，说容易烂龟是因为题太简单体现不出水平，尤其是在这学期midterm极难final极简单的情况下，几乎所有人都all in final，导致midterm高分根本没用，final只要有错就没A+，容错率很低。还有就是，这门课的考试是线上进行，但也有线下quiet room的名额。一定要尽量抢线下考的名额，否则可能会因为一些奇奇怪怪的原因收获penalty。

sections.teaching: Alex is an excellent instructor who explains everything clearly in PowerPoint slides. However, the lecture content is mostly limited to what is presented in the slides. Gibson provides more supplementary materials and focuses on key points rather than just the PowerPoint slides. He is also very humorous and often makes us laugh. However, sometimes he spends too much time discussing supplementary materials, and when the content is more challenging and requires more explanation, the progress may fall behind the scheduled timeline shown on the website. As a result, it can be difficult to review the material at times.
sections.grading:
Two grading methods.
24% midterm + 36% lab + 40% final
42% lab + 58% final
Lab: The lab component consists of seven labs in total, with three of them requiring hand-in submissions. While the labs are not particularly difficult, they can be time-consuming, and it is essential to ensure that everything works correctly and matches the marking scheme before submitting. A single error can significantly impact your lab grade, and the mean score is typically above 90.

Midterm: The midterm consists of two parts, with 25 minutes allotted for each section. However, the midterm in this semester was challenging, with tricky questions that resulted in a mean score below 50. The time is limited, and students cannot think deeply about the questions since they only have an average of 3-4 minutes per question.

Final: The final exam is also divided into two parts, with 40 minutes allotted for each section. The final exam is generally less challenging than the midterm, with a mean score above 65. The final exam includes longer questions that allow students more time to think about their answers.

Overall, it is relatively easy to achieve a normal grade in this course, but it can be challenging to earn an excellent grade (A/A+). A simple mistake can result in losing the entire mark for a question, and the competition among students is fierce.

sections.content:
I'd be inclined to call the course somewhat "advanced". If you have no programming background (e.g. no ICT in HKDSE and never coded much yourself), this course may be difficult simply because you need to think in a manner computers can understand.

While it is designed for complete newbies, the first few lectures were quite easy, literally calling and modifying a variable is all that was taught.

Then they got to dictionaries and recursions. I consider them "advanced" features since it's far from the most intuitive.

The course focuses on using the turtle library, a GUI library for drawing things. It's so basic I prefer using Scratch. Most course content focuses on turtle, so be prepared to live with it!

Overall, the content provides a nice base for anyone wanting to learn Python; you can probably do most things you would want to do if you import a few libraries and read their documentations.

LAM, Gibson is brilliant. Cracked so much jokes on the first lecture I watch some of his lectures as a podcast.

He joked about how, out of the 4 companies offering deals in the HKUST Electronics Fiesta, the 3 he tried all broke is some way. Has been the joke among my friends when we talk about how garbage some of those e-waste products are.
sections.grading:
Five graded "things":
3 Lab assignments:
Lab1: Guessing game
Code was basically provided in fully in the demo videos; bits of modifications will finish the assignment for full marks

Lab5: Music system
Focusing on iterating over an array, this task was quite time-consuming. Checking test-cases against expected output carefully basically guarantees full mark.

Lab6: Robot thinking
Solve a maze by hugging the right wall. The logic was basically: wall ahead, turn right.
If your robot can get through the test cases, you should be golden.

Mid-term:
Surprisingly challenging. I almost ran out of time in both parts. Rushing through the tasks meant I lost a few marks. One of my problem required more deduction than other possible sets (2 possible answers if you don't check what the output suggests)

Final:
Easy. Had 10-15 minutes left on both parts of 40 minutes each. Had enough time to type the entire program out to ensure that I haven't messed up dry-running code.

My marks:
100 for all 3 labs
83 for mid-term
100 for final

sections.content:
If you've spent a couple of hours watching Python tutorials on YouTube, you'll breeze through this course without breaking a sweat. The main part of the course is the Turtle module. It's not something you'll use for serious programming, but it's great for messing around with. You can make cool graphics by moving a "turtle" (pen) around the screen—it's like an interactive art project.

However, the Turtle module is like nothing in the real world of Python programming. If you're looking to learn Python in order to apply it to practical applications, this course just isn't it. In terms of difficulty, this course is as easy as it gets. It's designed for absolute beginners, so you won't feel overwhelmed at all. However, if you already have some programming experience, you might find it a bit too basic.
sections.teaching:
I gotta tell you, Prof. Gibson is hands down one of the coolest teachers I've ever had. Even though I already knew everything he talked about in class, I couldn't help but look forward to attending his lectures. This guy knows how to make learning fun :D

First of all, he is hilarious. He cracks jokes left and right, and it keeps the whole class entertained. He turns boring topics into comedy.

Secondly, I've never attended other lectures by other professors, but Prof. Gibson takes the time to break down and explain exam-styled questions. He provides us with strategies and clear explanations on how to approach and solve them effectively.

sections.content:
It's basic level programming. For people who have programming experience (like me), this will be an extremely easy course for you.

The most difficult part of this course is not making careless mistakes, such as submitting a wrong version of your code or forgetting to remove testing values you put in. These will cost you a lot of marks in your homework. I strongly urge you to double check your codes and files every time before submission.

The exams tests you on two things: how well you understand the Python functions and structures, and your eye for detail. Of course, you will need to know how Python works to get a good grade. However, the exam questions often sneak in cheeky “mistakes" that affects how the code functions and change the answer.

sections.grading:
Being an easy course comes with a huge drawback, which is a ridiculously skewed distribution curve. If you want to get A+, you will need to obtain near perfect scores in both homework and exams. Making small careless mistakes can easily drop your grade a level or two.

Made one mistake in one of my homework and a final exam question. Got an A+, so still pretty decent grade.

sections.content: Regarding the course content, COMP 1021 covers the necessary topics for students to gain a solid foundation in programming. The course material is divided into several modules, each of which focuses on a specific aspect of programming. The course website also provides a detailed syllabus, which gives students a clear understanding of what to expect from each module.
sections.teaching: In terms of teaching, the course has a team of experienced instructors who are well-versed in programming and have experience teaching the course. The instructors provide lectures, tutorials, and office hours to assist students in understanding the course material. The course also has a discussion forum where students can ask questions and engage with their peers.
sections.grading: In terms of grading, the course appears to have a rigorous evaluation system. According to the course website, the final grade is determined based on several components, including assignments, quizzes, exams, and a final project. This approach to grading ensures that students are evaluated on their overall understanding of the course material and their ability to apply it.
sections.workload: The workload for COMP 1021 appears to be moderate to high. The course involves several assignments, quizzes, exams, and a final project, which can be time-consuming. However, this workload is necessary to ensure that students understand the course material thoroughly and can apply it to practical situations.

It is because the weighting of the final exam is very high, so you need to be very careful in the exam. You lose 7-8 marks if you get one question wrong.

Overall, I got above 90 marks at the end of the course, but I still cannot get A range.

The midterm and final exams seem not to test the programming knowledge you learn in the class. In addition, there are so many words in the question but they are useless. sections.content:
For context, I had never EVER learned python before. I am a business major with no CS experience so it was a HUGE HUGE mistake to take COMP 1021. Everyone in this course is on the STEM track and therefore extremely smart and tech-savvy.

The presentations are helpful, I definitely recommend attending every single lecture. I stopped attending midway and I think that's what caused my downfall. Ask a ton of questions whenever you can because you WILL be left hanging most of the time.

It gets a LOT more difficult after the midterm. Prior to the midterm its more basic, primary content. But towards the end of the semester it gets really really advanced and the pace of teaching is so so quick.
sections.teaching:
Rossiter is hilarious, I loved LOVED his accent and teaching style. He has a British accent and is quite animated at times.

He picks out students at random to answer questions in class just to put you on the spot a little bit. But no harm if you don't answer, a lot of people usually don't know.
sections.grading:
It's not bad per se, but if you get a bad grade, you'll be screwed. Because for most STEM students this course is basic, the curve is INSANE. I got around a 75% and only ended up with a C.

I got below 0.5 SD below mean on both midterm and final. I got 100% in the first two labs, and 60% on the third lab.

If you don't work hard and dedicate at least 4-5 hours to this course every week, you will be royally f'ed.

The grading is done two ways:
1. The midterm is worth around 30%, final 50% , and labs 20%
2. The final worth 60% and labs 40%

You should focus on doing well in the midterm so it doesn't all fall upon the final.
sections.workload:
There's no attendance grading so up to you if you wanna go.

There are 3 graded labs in the semester, all fairly self explanatory if you watch the lab videos. I screwed up on the last one about music production because i didn't attend those lectures nor did I go to the Lab TA for help. I cannot emphasize enough on reaching out for help.

There are 2 exams- a midterm and final. Both are quite difficult and very difficult to complete on time. I didn't finish both times. I recommend going through the examples online and the sample papers ESPECIALLY. Please do the sample papers if you want a good grade. Learn from my mistakes rip.

sections.grading:
Unfortunately, new courses sometimes have an odd quality to them. It would be the enrolled pupils in this instance. For whatever reason, the class's pupils are very talented and competitive this semester, which produces a relatively high mean and a small SD.

The following is the grading system:

Participation in class (10%, in-class Canvas)
- Homework (4 sets, 10%)
- Group Project (20% of the total grade, 5% report, 5% peer review, and 10% poster presentation) (You will forfeit the 5% report if your peer assessment score is less than 30%.) (You will forfeit the 10% poster presentation fee if you do not attend the poster presentation.)
- The midterm test (30%)
- The final test (30%)

sections.content: The course mainly covers the basics of python programming as well as teaching turtle graphics. Topics covered include, but are not limited to, logic operators, loops, slicing, lists, tuples, strings, and recursion. There are powerpoint slides that help you understand the course materials as well as interactive programming exercises, so the content is fairly easy to comprehend even if you have no previous  knowledge of programming. Even if you fail to
sections.teaching: Dr. Alex Lam is a easy-to-approach professor, as he is friendly and willing to answer your questions even after the lessons. He also reviews memes before the lessons start to help lighten the mood and engage with his students.
sections.grading:
The grading system is written very clearly on the course' page. There are two ways to calculate your final grade: the first one includes your midterm grades while the second one only includes your final exam marks and assignment grades. The exams are not that hard, but if you are not careful and make some silly mistakes it could cost you a lot of marks.
Final exam:
- average 71.3
- standard deviation 20.7
- maximum 100
- minimum 4
Mid term:
- average 62.1
- standard deviation 24.1
- maximum 100
- minimum 7
I got a 92 in my final exam and a 77 in my midterm, so I used the second calculation method for my grades and got an A. A-range is not hard as long as you submit all your assignment and are careful, but competition is fierce at the top so getting A+ is not that easy.

This course should be named:
Introduction to Python OR Introduction to Turtle Graphics

I think it is not too good to start for students that would like to pursue their career in computer science since this is too easy. Students that are passionate in the field should be able to learn all the contents of the course in half a month instead of three months.

It is not bad for other students to learn some programming skills since this is indeed the trend of the Information Age.

I think Prof. Alex Lam teaches quite well. His teaching can be understood really easily.

I don't know much to comment on because I already knew Python before I took this course but I see him answering questions using Cantonese, Mandarin, and English after class, so I feel like it wouldn't be hard for students with no programming background to understand.
sections.grading:
I have some background in programming so I think the course is not too hard to get a good grade. But it is still very easy to lose points in examinations due to carelessness. I didn't get full marks in the mid-term examination because of that. Luckily, the second scheme doesn't count mid-term, and I got full marks in all labs and final examinations so I get A+.

This semester's mean mark is so high for the final examination and turns out the cutoff is very very high. I would say I am just lucky enough to get full marks this time. But the grade is still very bad for most people.

I recommend you take the exams in the quiet rooms even if they give you the option to take that on Zoom (if you are just taking that yourself:)) because it is really easy to get mark penalties if you do it on Zoom.
sections.workload:
There are only three hand-in labs in the whole semester. They only took you several hours each even if you didn't learn programming before.

If you have learnt programming before and understand, you can finish them easily in one hour each, which is approximately zero workload.

Be careful about the deadline though. Don't miss the deadline for the hand-in labs. It would be an automatic zero if you miss the deadline. And check the marking scheme carefully so you don't lose points.

sections.content:
This course teaches some primary python language stuff while using it to teach you some basic concepts about computer science, including:

3. for loop

5. function
6. recursion
And it mainly uses the stuff called turtle graphics to teach you about these concepts.

Please be noted that the textbook is mainly useless since the lecture slides can provide a better understanding than the textbook.....so expect you are wealthy and want to spend money on some extra stuff. save that money and have a coffee.
sections.teaching: Professor David's Teaching is outstanding, one of the best at HKUST. He is chilling, and his teaching style is quite funny, which makes getting the concept relatively easy. In addition, lecture notes are well structured, so you can quickly get ideas. Finally, assistants by TAs in the lab are handy. One-on-one assistance is provided with good homework content so that you can quickly locate your missing concept and resolve it with the TAs in the lab. So I think you should attend this section.
sections.grading: I have to give a D on the grading since the grading has become quite tight this year; I don't trust the senior who said this is a good grade course since the grading has been changed. You will face some of the masters in python taking this course, and YOU WILL BE Fed if you are a newbie. So I suggest you take the code camp before taking this course.
sections.workload: This course has a reasonable workload since very few lab projects have to be submitted in this course. Moreover, the projects are easy since the templates are given, and you must fill in the fixing code. Assistants are also provided so you can get help if you are trapped. But I give a B grade since you will have tremendous pressure by having zero mistakes in the homework so that you will not miss a lot of marks and get a poor grade since the mean is relatively high and the SD is relatively small. You also have to take a lot of past papers to get familiar with the exam mode.

sections.content: The content of the class is very simple. It is the basic content of computer, so students without computer foundations can understand it.
sections.teaching: rossiter speaks very vividly and passionately. However, the difficulty of the content of the class and the content of the exam are too different. The exam is very unfriendly to students who have no computer foundation at all. Since you made the exam questions so difficult, shouldn't the class be more difficult? In the end, I just had to study on my own for the final based on the questions from previous years.
sections.grading:
This is the most sb part of the class. A fucking bunch of people have studied computers before. The result is a particularly bad grade given. Don't you fucking call a basic computer class supposed to be for students with no computer skills? This course is required for many non-SENG students. As a result, it's mixed with a bunch of students who have the basics and those who eventually want to major in computer science. How can we compare this class together when we all place different levels of importance on it?
It is difficult for non-SENG students or students with basic knowledge to do well in this course. And more importantly, the way the grade is given in this class is also very retarded. There are two ways to give grades, one counts as a midterm grade and one does not, but the final grade and the usual work will account for a much larger percentage. These two ways seem to give us more opportunities. But in reality, there is only one way to get a good grade. That is to get a high grade at the end of the period. To be clear the grade for this class is basically just the final. Even if your midterm and regular assignments are high, once you don't play well at the end of the semester your grade in this class is bound to suck. Because no matter how you do the math, the percentage at the end of the period is the largest. Also the grades in this class are too damn concentrated. A- and B- are less than ten points apart. Even if you can get a few points above MEAN, you can only get a B-. To put it bluntly, the grades given are really fucking outrageous.
Finally, students without basic knowledge are advised not to enroll in this course in the fall. There are too many students and seniors who have taken computer science. It is recommended to enroll in the spring and you should be better off.
sections.workload: It doesn't look very big. There are only a few times the lab has to be completed. But because the class lectures are too easy, you have to find a way to study on your own in order to cope with the exam. Do past topics or study python related videos online. This will increase the workload substantially.

sections.content:
I personally have no text programming background at all (only block programming experience). The first few topics were all fundamental, so if you didn't fully understand it, you wouldn't be able to understand the succeeding lessons. Most of the lessons after the midterm just build on your fundamental knowledge by making it more complex.

There were 31 PowerPoint Presentation files (including introductory ones) and each PPT usually corresponds to one topic.

There are both explanations and examples provided in the PPTs. They oversimplify many terms and make analogies to help better understand the topics (which is extremely helpful if you do not have any experience with programming, but it might seem too easy to those who have experience).

However, the midterm and final exams are completely different from the labs and interactive examples. They are much longer and usually don't have much examples to refer to in the PPTs. I STRONGLY RECOMMEND doing pass papers AND the interactive examples to strengthen your knowledge and become comfortable with the exam format.

Many questions can be overwhelming and complicated that require you to read long lines of code and try to critically interpret it without putting it into python.
sections.teaching:
I attended almost all of the lectures and I can say that this course can definitely be learned alone. The lecture did help to supplement my learning but because most of the information about each topic are thoroughly explained in the PPTs, it's easy to learn on your own.

Professor Li does a good job at teaching the course as it was made to be taught - as an introduction to computer science for those who have no background knowledge on it. She can be a bit repetitive sometimes, but they can also serve as important reminders for beginners. She rarely talks about things that are not included in the PPT and she entertains questions well. She is very responsive and easy to approach.

I took Elective A (Database), instead of Elective D (Software Development), in my DSE ICT and got a 5* (in fact 0.5% to 5**) in 2022 but I didn't find this course tough to study.

But please be noted that this course does not require you to have a programming background and it starts from zero. Therefore, I don't think that it is difficult to catch up if you have no ICT knowledge.

However, I think that there is too much content about turtle drawings in python instead of real problem-solving algorithms. This is the only minus point I think about the content of this course.

sections.workload:
There are two lectures (each 50 minutes) and one voluntary lab session (110 minutes) per week.

No attendance is taken, you can skip all the lectures and lab sessions if you can handle it. Video recording of lectures is available. Lab sessions are just for you to ask questions about the lab work while actually the website of the lab has already given you plenty of guidelines.

The only workload is the weekly lab work, only _ out of _ need submission, with marking scheme provided before submission deadline. The only tough stuff are some lab works like designing a game with python requiring you to think a lot.

Overall workload rate: A (about 2.8 credit)

Typing skills and reading speed will be of great importance since you're unable to copy some of the code from exams, but you're allowed to type them out and run them. The grading for the assignments and the weekly labs are fair. Especially easy to ace and get high grades. The exam is definitely hard and challenging and does require a good understanding and ability to apply the content.

The curve is fair for the final and midterm and there are various grading formulas and the highest grade is chosen after all this. I think that is the bright side to this. Doing well on the labs and midterm would help you compensate for a shitty final.

For me the final went terribly, it was one of the worst exams I could ahve imagined. The irony was that i did infact revise and spend hours flipping through my notes and practicing. since my labs were all complete and I ended up with aa  100% there and my midterm was satisfactory, the final didn't hurt me too much. sections.grading:
Labs:
Grading for this course was all over the place and fairly poor overall. The labs make up between 36% & 42% of your final grade which is very heavy given that basically everyone gets 100% on them. The grading for most of the labs is automatic so make sure to read the instructions carefully.

Midterm:
The midterm was pretty easy making up 24% or 0% of your grade.  Since the average is fairly high I studied for it and got a satisfactory grade.

Final:
The final is HELL and is more of a reading comprehension exam than anything else. It makes up between 40% to 58% of your grade so you definitely don't want to mess that one up. The explanation for the questions is extremely long so your gonna have a serious advantage if you are a fast reader & can type fast aswell. I personally wasn't able to complete the final because I'm a fairly slow reader and straight-up didn't have enough time to read the last 2 questions.

Grading formula:
The only reaming thing about the grading in this course is that it uses 2 formulas to calculate your grade & takes the higher result of the 2 as your final score.

Formula 1: Midterm 24% , Lab 36%, Final 40%
Formula 2: Midterm 0%, Lab 42%, Final 58%

The content is very comprehensive. It covers a lot of the basics and it definitely trains a programming mindset. The focus will be on topics like if/else statements, loops, functions, lists, dictionaries, recursion, and a brief intro to objects. Things like these are gonna pop up in other programming languages so it really gives you that mindset. There is also a large focus on using Turtle Graphics, so make sure you're familiar with that.

They definitely teach you from zero and assume you don't have prior knowledge in programming, so don't worry if you don't know programming but want to enroll in this course. I didn't know programming before this course and the contents were quite easy to grasp.
sections.teaching:
Sung was amazing. Some other reviews on here complain about his accent but I think it was fine. It sounded kinda cute too. Sung makes his lectures interesting and I've never slept in his lectures. I couldn't say the same about other lecturers. Sung also interacts with the class by asking us questions. He also does demonstrations in class which makes what we're learning very clear.

Big props to David (course coordinator) too and actually the whole COMP1021 team for making all the course materials readily available online. The revision materials are super comprehensive, super neat, and super easy to find. There are also lots of interactive exercises on the website for us to familiarize ourselves with the concepts we've learned and put what we've learned into practice, which is very nice because education is supposed to be two-wayed.

If you are a fast learner, I'd definitely suggest Sung. He doesn't assume you have prior programming knowledge, but he goes through content faster than David and Gibson. He also teaches extra things that might help improve your programming skills, which is a bonus if you're thinking of learning more COMP in the future. But if you are not a fast learner and think you're bad with things like programming, I'd suggest David and Gibson. I've sat in their lectures before and they go through concepts slowly, but more clearly. They're probably the pick for people who think they might struggle.

There are two grading methods: 24% midterm + 36% lab + 40% final OR 42% lab + 58% final.

I'd definitely suggest taking the midterm because the midterm is often a lot easier than the final.

For lab assignments, the mark scheme is very clear so it is not hard to get 100. But then again almost everyone gets 100 for lab so it doesn't give you much of an edge.

The final is kind of like the be-all and end-all. Even though the exams are online and open-book, they make it purposefully short so Googling your answers would be a waste of time. The final had a mean of like 48 so I guess a lot of people tripped up on that, not because the questions were hard, but because of the time.

I will not reveal my grade but I have to say I was quite happy with what I got, considering I have no programming background prior to taking the course.

sections.content:
This course teaches Python 3 using turtle library. You can think of it as teaching programming with the help of graphical representation. Most of the concept will be represented by pictures within the ppt or using example programs.

Lecture:
No attendance is required, 1.5 hours(or 1hr forgot) per lecture, 2 lecture per week. with 1 lab but is not mandatory to attend if you don't have any questions to ask.

Materials, content:
1. basic syntax (indent, variable naming restriction)
2. printing things to console.
3. variables (Gibson teaches this concept pretty well with a gentle learning curve throughout the course)
4. if else (using graphics on the screen, so wont be a problem if you understand logics)
5. loops (for while)
6. File Read write
sections.teaching:
Gibson teaches python in a fun way by providing examples outside the reading materials. Even if you dont read the ppt beforehand you should be able to understand most of the concept within the lecture.
You can ask questions after class using email any time, but never use canvas, as they might not be able to receive your questions.
You can also ask question in class and he will answer you by modifying the in class example he created, should be enough for most students to understand the concept.
sections.grading:
Better be prepared to get a B or C if you dont have programming experience. If you dont have any experience, try to get full marks on **all** hand-in labs. (total 3 out of 5)
If you are familiar with python, watch out for variable name and don't trust the comments within the exam or midterm, they can be fake.

36% lab
24% midterm
40% final

or

42% lab
0%  midterm
58% final

The course will choose the method with the higher score for you.

The final exam is hard, because the time constrain is pretty tight. Also, double-check the answer and don't fall into some traps. Then, you will be fine.

sections.content:
This course is very easy for those who have taken HKDSE ICT before. Python is no doubt much easier than the programming language (i.e. C language) I have taken in secondary school. If you have taken ICT in secondary school like me, then I have to say congratulations, you would probably grasp all materials really quick without much revision.

(The website of the course is the following one:

https://course.cse.ust.hk/comp1021

)

This course involves the following things:
-2 lectures each week, 13 weeks in total
-8 labs (include both 3 hand-in labs and 5 non-hand-in labs)
-1 practice exam (help you to get familiar with the format of midterm exam, it does not count towards your final grade)
-1 real mid-term exam
-1 real final exam

Here is the syllabus:

-Course Details; Getting Started with Python

-Beginning to Program Python

-Introduction to Turtle Graphics

-Making Decisions

-Loops

-Basic Turtle Graphics Summary; Example of a Nested Loop

-Using For Loops; Using For Loops with Graphics

-Midterm Details; Lists, Tuples and Strings

-Handling Repeating Patterns; More on Loops

-Using Logic; Slicing

-Slicing, cont.; More on Lists and Strings

-Functions; Dictionaries

-Handling of Data Types

-Turtle Shapes; Creating Turtles; Clicking and Dragging Turtles

-Handling Key Presses; Clicking on the Turtle Window; An Example Game - Circles Game; Large Turtle Graphics Summary

-More on Functions

-More on Operators

-Text and File Handling

-Final Exam Details; The Coordinate System; Understanding Colours

-State Diagrams; Objects

-Objects, continued; Recursion

-Recursion, continued

Here are the names for the 8 labs in this semester:

Lab 0: Hello World and Introduction to Turtle Graphics
Lab 1: Guessing Game
Lab 2: Turtle Sketchbook (*Hand-in Lab)
Lab 3: Fireworks
Lab 4: Jigsaw

sections.content:
In this course you learn python programming from scratch, so it starts off with the basics, such as setting up IDLE on your computer.
The main topics in this course were:
- If statements
- For/While Loops (and nested loops)
- List, Tuples, Strings and slicing
- Data types and operators
- Functions
- Dictionaries
- Text and File handling
- State Diagrams
- Recursion
- Turtle graphics:
    - Moving/rotating turtle, drawing stuff with it
    - Objects
    - Creating turtles
    - Interacting with the turtles/turtle window

All in all, you could say the labs test your ability to apply programming concepts and follow instructions, while the exams test your ability to be perceptive and solve problems within time constraints.
sections.teaching: The professor teaches in an interesting way, as he doesn’t completely rely on slides and may often use his own examples or explanations. The slides are anyways quite simple and easy to refer back to when needed. There are regular polls in class to help you ensure that you are understanding the concepts, while the TAs are available to answer any questions you may have about exams/labs.
sections.grading:
There are 2 different grading schemes:
Mid term 24% Final 40% Lab 36%
MT 0% Final 58% Lab 42%

The labs are relatively easy so the mean is quite high (between 90 and 100%)
The mean for midterm was a little less than 80%, while the mean for the final exam was around 47%.

Since this course is quite easy for all the people who have done programming before, in the exams there are many long questions with code that cannot be copied, so you have to mainly use critical thinking/problem solving skills.

It becomes easier to miss certain parts of the code, and since there was barely enough time to recheck, I made a few silly mistakes in both exams. It is important to read the code to make sure you don’t fall for any of the trick questions, as you don’t get partial marks for any of them - if you get a question wrong you lose all of the marks.
sections.workload:
For someone who has done programming before, the workload is not that high. There are only 3 simple hand-in labs, all with instructions or videos to guide you step-by-step. You can do the labs at your own pace, and even finish and hand them in before the scheduled lab sessions (personally I never attended the lab sessions).

The other labs are ones that you can do in your free time, they are not compulsory, but knowledge of what they are about may help out in the final exam.

Revising for the exams is not hard as they provide past papers and interactive examples for you to work on and play around with.

You are also free to attend other lectures, the schedule for this course is quite flexible.

sections.grading:
Two grading methods.

24% midterm + 36% lab + 40% final
OR
42% lab + 58% final

There are 7 labs + one intro lab, 3 of which are graded out of 100.

Labs are easy, but be extremely careful and check each case carefully as often there are no partial marks and one silly mistake causing your program to crash in a test case can cost you 20% of the lab score. (true story D:). The labs usually have a mean of 90-100 with s.d 8-10.

The midterm is fairly easy, as long as you're somewhat careful and double-check your answers. If you've done programming, you should have at least half the time to check your answers. Exams are done remotely this semester. Mean was 71.9 with s.d about 21.4.

However, the final is hell. There is barely enough time for you to check your answers. The questions are extremely weird and try to trick you, for example by multiplying a number by 2 but they made the number a string instead of an int. You have to be extremely careful. The mean this semester was 48.57 with s.d 19.29.

Alternatively, you can see the final as a typing test and just type out all the code they don't let you copy. If you are fast enough at typing (at least 90-100wpm) then this is actually a viable option for you, and makes the final much less stressful.

My scores:
Lab 1 - 80%
Lab 2 - 100%
Lab 3 - 100%
Mterm: 90%
Final: 100% (after grading change)

Overall: ~97% (definitely enough for A+)

It is quite difficult to get an A/A+ even if you've already programmed before, because the exams basically are a human aptitude test or a geometry test disguised as a Python exam. There are only one or two questions where you use Python to solve a problem. They purposely make the tests tricky and weird because too many people going into this course can already program so they had to "fix the curve" somehow

Really friendly professor, and is willing to discuss more advanced topics that are not in the syllabus after the lecture. Very quick in replying to emails. He sometimes sends us emails with reminders, further clarifications and the video recording link if he overran the lecture.

Dr Alex Lam is a good professor for complete beginners in my opinion, but not so much if you have prior programming experience (since you could read the notes instead if so). I attended all lectures and most of the time I just worked on my own programs.

For beginners, this teaching style might be easier to follow. He often starts with a quick recap of the last lecture before moving on to the content of that lecture, so that you'll remember it. He mostly follows the slides and then demonstrates the concepts in the Python shell.

= Differences between instructors (From the slides of the first lecture) =
You can participate in other lecture sessions even if you are not enrolled in them, plus lecture videos are available on the course site for everyone anyway

- Dr Alex Lam & Prof Wilfred Ng: Teach using slides, and using mainly examples on the course site
- Prof Kim Sung Hun: Teach using slides, but using new illustrations and examples beyond those on the course site
- Prof David Rossiter & Prof Gibson Lam: Teach using other things instead of slides, and using new illustrations and examples beyond those on the course site

- Maximum: 100

The exams are more like a test of meticulousness since it is very easy to miss something or be mistaken (especially under stress), which results in a wrong answer, which is 5-10 marks lost per question since there's only one answer per question and no partial scores.

Both exams are online (due to mixed mode), sent to you as two PDF files, and answers are submitted through Canvas. There is a short break between part A and part B.

You can only use Python, the COMP1021 Course site and sites that do not have communication features (Like the official Python documentation).

Technically you could type out all of the code (even if you can't directly copy from the PDF), though I find understanding the logic first, then coding an abbreviated version of it to be better.

- A: 7 questions in 25 minutes
- B: 5 questions in 25 minutes
Final:
- A: 9 questions in 40 minutes
- B: 9 questions in 40 minutes

(Due to mixed mode:)
There are on-campus seats that you could reserve so that you don't need to set up the Zoom camera (as you are supervised in person instead). I did it on-campus for midterm and on Zoom for the final, and I'd prefer to reserve a seat. Be sure to request it as soon as it is available as they are very limited. sections.content:
Basic Python programming. Everything is very straightforward. The course focuses on fundamental programming concepts like data types, operators, loops, lists, functions and etc. It would be super easy for students with programming to understand the course content, not so difficult for students who don't have programming experience though.

Pay more attention to loops, functions and recursion. Make sure you are very clear about how they work on Python, otherwise you may struggle in some of the labs and the exams. Also pay more attention to Python-specific content like difference between lists and tuples, slicing, dictionaries and turtles. These concepts would be frequently asked in exams.

1. Mid term 24%,  Final 40%, Labs 36%
2. Mid term 0%, Final 58%, Labs 42%

Mid term is fairly easy, score high in mt to guarantee a good paper grade.

Final is of course more difficult. Final this semester was obviously harder than past papers (maybe because it was online exam). Practise how to trace codes to save time and get correct answers in complex questions that mix different concepts together.

sections.content:
This course gives you a basic and introductory look at Python.
Teaches you things like for, while loops, if statements, also Turtle graphics. They also provide a lot of notes, pdf, and sometime even interactive examples. The labs are actually interesting and fun.

If you have any programming experience before this course, even if it's another language, you should be able to get by with a breeze. If you have close to no programming background like me, the content is actually perfect to getting you started on Python.

Whether or not the knowledge taught, especially Turtle graphics, will be useful in the future is honestly debatable, but the course does set a good foundation for programming and it certainly teaches you the logical thinking that programming needs.
sections.teaching: David was straightforward, clear in his teaching, and sometimes he's quite humorous in his lectures, joking about the content or the TA. It did make the course a lot more enjoyable from what could have been a dry and maybe daunting experience for some.
sections.grading:
This course in spring 2020-2021 was conducted online and I've already forgotten a lot of the specific details so beware xD.

I believe there were 4 hand-in labs and they were easy to get full marks in, given the amount of instruction and guidelines. The most complex lab I would say is the robot getting out of a maze because it does require a clear, logical mindset because you are dealing will a lot of if-statements, and the code also had to be robust enough to complete most mazes (They test your code by giving the robot random mazes). You also get quite some time to complete these lab. So generally speaking, you should be able to get high marks here.

The mid-term and final on the other hand were quite challenging.
Most questions revolves around code analysis. So basically you have the decide whether that given code will execute without error, what that output might be, etc. We were allowed to copy and run certain codes given, but more challenging questions forbid that. You really have to understand what most line of codes are doing and how they interact with each other, while painting a picture in your head of what the output might be (because it often involves Turtle graphics) to be able to do more challenging questions.

I would say the time given in these exam was quite limited, but it is possible to do all questions with enough practice of coding stuff / doing past papers.

I'm not exactly sure about grading, but it might be heavily skewed by people who already have programming experience.

In the end, I got full marks on all labs, except the robot maze one.
I got only 1 question wrong in mid-term and full marks on final.
So I got A+.
sections.workload: The workload was light, the labs were easy to do within a week's time and the labs were already helping you practise for the exams. However I would say your grade is proportional to the amount of time you spend revising / practising / programming (whatever you plan to do).

Basic programming concepts taught using Python language, like input/output, variables, logic operators, if statement and loops, data structures, recursion. If you have taken ICT in secondary school you would've already learnt almost everything.

List of chapters:

Chapter 3: Comment, Variables and Text
Chapter 4: Variable Types and Operators
Chapter 5: Making Decisions
Chapter 6: Looping
Chapter 7: Finding Repeating Patterns

sections.teaching: Gibson is a very fun and good lecturer! He is very passionate about the teaching material and his voice is very clear in the lesson. He manages to keep everything fun and engaging for all students. Even if I had learnt most of the concept already in secondary school he still managed to make the lesson interesting for me! Definitely recoomand Gibson as best lecturer!
sections.grading:
For a student who had already studied ICT in secondary school or someone who are interested in STEM, the assignment and exam question won't be hard for you. There isn't really tricky question meant to trick you into losing marks and all the question makes sense.

Also there are two grading system that are meant to assist students who slip up in midterm. You don't need to worry about getting a very bad grade even if you perform badly at midterm.

Grading scheme 1:
Assignment 1 + 2: 25% + 25%
Midterm: 35%
Online assignment: 15%

Grading scheme 2:
Assignment 1 + 2: 35% + 35%
Midterm: 10%
Online assignment: 20%

The better grading scheme will be automatically used for you to get the best result.

Also there are bonus marks for student who answer question in lecture for a maximum of 3 marks.

I get full marks in both assignment 1 + 2 and the online one. For midterm I get 90/100. I also get 3 extra marks for answering question in lecture. Got an A+ so I would say it is very good grade course.
sections.workload:
The workload is very light. There are lab session but they don't require attendence and are just glorified copy and paste work where you follow the lab assistance's code.

The two programming assignment are basically the same thing. You can copy almost all of the program code from the lecture note. Since the skeleton code is provided, it is basically fill in the blanks until you get the results.

You have ample time to finish the little things that you need to do and you can easily get full marks just by getting the needed output.

sections.content: The course is very friendly for people with zero computer science background. All content is comprehensive and easy to understand. Final is way more difficult than mid-term, and don't ever trust the difficulties of past papers.

sections.content:
This course teaches basic programming with Python using turtle graphics, which is a Python library that allows you to draw things.
Refers to other reviews for more details of the course.

The content of the course is really simple and straightforward. In most lectures, you only need to learn a few lines of new functions, and you can understand everything easily just by looking at the lecture slides. The only topics that take a little more time to understand are object and recursion.
sections.teaching: Cecia is a nice lecturer and she teaches every topic in the course with great details and lots of examples, so you can understand everything easily even if you have never tried programming before. She is also willing to answer questions patiently after class. The lectures are a bit boring though because the explanation of things takes too long, especially for topics which are not hard to understand.
sections.grading:
There is 2 grading scheme for this course:
Midterm 24%, Lab projects 36%, Final exam 40%  or
Midterm 0%, Lab projects 42%, Final exam 58%
The final score would be the highest out of these two calculation methods.

Lab projects: They are just simple programming assignments, and for the 7 lab assignments only 3 of them are hand in labs that count for grades. For each of the lab would provide a step-by-step explanation of nearly everything on the website. Also, you can ask for help from the TAs during tutorial sessions to finish those Labs. This result in a very high average score for the Lab projects:
lab 2 average 97.4
lab 4 98.4
lab 6 90.9
Since the significant portion of labs in grades and the high average of the labs, it is very very important to hand in the labs on time. Missing one of the labs would cause a drop of at least 2 subgrades.
(Btw remember NOT to share your lab codes with your classmate and friends, I heard that some people have their lab score voided with grade penalty in addition because of code plagiarism)

For the exams, they are open book and you can visit the course webpage look for notes, also we are allowed to use Python during the exam. Some of the codes can be copied while you need to manually type the codes for some. Having fast typing speed is definitely an advantage in the exam.

Midterm exam covers the first half of the course and is quite simple, for most questions you can just type the code provided and then obtain the answer. here are the stats:
Maximum: 100
Minimum: 13
Mean: 74.6
SD: 17.9

The final exam covers everything and is significantly more difficult than the midterm, not only due to the increased difficulty of the last few topics, the complexity of the questions also raised a lot. There is a question that requires you to copy a large chunk of code by hand, and there are also questions that provide you more than 20 options and ask you to pick the correct one. This makes the whole exam so demanding. The average of the final is notably lower than the midterm. Stats:
Maximum: 100
Minimum: 0
Mean: 60.59
SD: 22.28

Overall I think the grading of this course is great. I got a full mark for labs, +1sd for midterm, and +1.8sd for final. Finally get an A+
sections.workload: The workload is near nil. The first two labs only take around an hours to finish and the last one takes 2 hours. Also the exams are open book, which means you only need to briefly know the functions taught, without the need to memorize them.
